caaba.etymology: Ar. ka'ban, let, a square building, fr. ka'b cube

cabal.etymology: F. cabale cabal, cabala LL. cabala cabala, fr. Heb. qabbaleh reception, tradition, mysterious doctrine, fr. qabal to take or receive, in Piël qibbel to abopt (a doctrine).

cabbage.etymology: OE. cabage, fr. F. cabus headed (of cabbages), chou cobus headed cabbage, cabbage head; cf. It. capuccio a little head, cappuccio cowl, hood, cabbage, fr. capo head, L. caput, or fr. It. cappa cape. See Chiff, Cape.

cabin.etymology: OF. caban, fr. W. caban booth, cabin, dim. of cab cot, tent; or fr. F. cabane, cabine, LL. cabanna, perh. from the Celtic.

cabinet.etymology: F., dim. of cabine or cabane. See Cabin, n.

cable.etymology: F. Câble,m LL. capulum, caplum, a rope, fr. L. capere to take; cf. D., Dan., & G. rabel, from the French. See Capable.

caboose.etymology: Cf. D. kabuis, kombuis, Dan. kabys, Sw. kabysa, G. kabuse a little room or hut. The First part of the word seems to be allied to W. cab cabin, booth. Cf. Cabin.

cabotage.etymology: F. cabotage, fr. caboter to sail along the coast; cf. Sp. cabo cape.

cabriolet.etymology: F., dim. of cabriole a leap, caper, from It. capriola, fr. dim. of L. caper he-goat, capra she-goat. This carriage is so called from its skipping lightness. Cf. Cab, Caper a leap.

cacao.etymology: Sp., fr. Mex. kakahuatl. Cf. Cocoa, Chocolate

cache.etymology: F., a hiding place, fr. cacher to conceal, to hide.

cackle.etymology: OE. cakelen; cf. LG. kakeln, D. kakelen, G. gackeln, gackern; all of imitative origin. Cf. Gagle, Cake to cackle.

roots.meaning: A suffix used as a characteristic termination of chemical radicals; as in ethyl, carbonyl, hydroxyl, etc.
A suffix denoting the art of writing or describing; also, the writing or description itself; a treatise; as, calligraphy, biography, geography.

cacuminal.etymology: L. cacumen, cacuminis, the top, point.

caddy.etymology: Earlier spelt catty, fr. Malay kati a weight of 11/3 pounds. Cf. Catty.

cadence.etymology: OE. cadence, cadens, LL. cadentia a falling, fr. L. cadere to fall; cf. F. cadence, It. cadenza. See Chance.

cadent.etymology: L. cadens, -entis, p. pr. of cadere to fall.

cadet.etymology: F. cadet a younger or the youngest son or brother, dim. fr. L. caput head; i. e., a smaller head of the family, after the first or eldest. See Chief, and cf. Cad.

cadge.etymology: Cf. Scot. cache, caich, cadge, to toss, drive, OE. cachen to drive, catch, caggen to bind, or perh. E. cage. Cf. Cadger.

cadger.etymology: From Cadge, v. t., cf. Codger.

cadre.etymology: F. cadre, It. quadro square, from L. quadrum, fr. quatuor four.

caducous.etymology: L. caducus falling, inclined to fall, fr. cadere to fall. See Cadence.

caecilian.etymology: L. caecus blind. So named from the supposed blindness of the species, the eyes being very minute.

caesium.etymology: NL., from L. caesius bluish gray.

caesura.etymology: L. caesura a cutting off, a division, stop, fr. caedere, caesum, to cut off. See Concise.

cage.etymology: F. cage, fr. L. cavea cavity, cage, fr. cavus hollow. Cf. Cave, n., Cajole, Gabion.

cahoot.etymology: Perhaps fr. f. cohorte a a company or band.

cairn.etymology: Gael. carn, gen. cairn, a heap: cf. Ir. & W. carn.

caisson.etymology: F., fr. caisse, case, chest. See 1st Case.

caitiff.etymology: OE. caitif, cheitif, captive, miserable, OF. caitif, chaitif, captive, mean, wretched, F. chétif, fr. L. captivus captive, fr. capere to take, akin to E. heave. See Heave, and cf. Captive.

cajole.etymology: F. cajoler, orig., to chatter like a bird in a cage, to sing; hence, to amuse with idle talk, to flatter, from the source of OF. goale, jaiole, F. geôle, dim. of cage a cage. See Cage, Jail.

cake.etymology: OE. cake, kaak; akin to Dan. kage, Sw. & Icel. kaka, D. koek, G.kuchem, OHG. chuocho.

calabash.etymology: Sp. calabaza, or Pg. calaba, caba (cf. F. Calebasse), lit., a dry gourd, fr. Ar. qar', fem., a kind of gourd + aibas dry.

calamary.etymology: LL. calamarium inkstand, fr. L. calamus a reed pen: cf. F. calmar, calemar, pen case, calamar.

calamine.etymology: F. calamine, LL. calamina, fr. L. Cabmia. See Cadmia.

calamint.etymology: OE. calamint, calemente (cf. F. calament) fr. L. calamintha, Gr. Mint.

calamity.etymology: L. calamitas, akin to in- columis unharmed: cf. F. calamité

roots.meaning: A prefix from Eng. prep. in, also from Lat. prep. in, meaning in, into, on, among; as, inbred, inborn, inroad; incline, inject, intrude. In words from the Latin, in- regularly becomes il- before l, ir- before r, and im- before a labial; as, illusion, irruption, imblue, immigrate, impart. In- is sometimes used with an simple intensive force.

calash.etymology: F. calèche; of Slavonic origin; cf. Bohem. kolesa, Russ. koliaska calash, koleso, kolo, wheel.

calcareous.etymology: L. calcarius pertaining to lime. See Calx.

calceolaria.etymology: NL., fr. L. calceolarius shoemaker, fr. calceolus, a dim. of calceus shoe.

calcic.etymology: L. calx, calcis, lime: cf. F. calcique.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

calcine.etymology: F. calciner, fr. L. calx, calcis, lime. See Calx.

calcium.etymology: NL., from L. calx, calcis, lime; cf F. calcium. See Calx.

calculate.etymology: L, calculatus, p. p. of calculate, fr. calculus a pebble, a stone used in reckoning; hence, a reckoning, fr. calx, calcis, a stone used in gaming, limestone. See Calx.

calculation.etymology: OE. calculation, fr. L. calculatio; cf. OF. calcucation.

calculus.etymology: L, calculus. See Calculate, and Calcule.

caldron.etymology: OE. caldron, caudron, caudroun, OF. caudron, chauderon, F. chaudron, an aug. of F. chaudière, LL. caldaria, fr. L. caldarius suitable for warming, fr. caldus, calidus, warm, fr. calere to be warm; cf. Skr. çra to boil. Cf. Chaldron, Calaric, Caudle.

calefacient.etymology: L. calefaciens p. pr. of calefacere to make warm; calere to be warm + facere to make.

calendar.etymology: OE. kalender, calender, fr. L. kalendarium an interest or account book (cf. F. calendrier, OF. calendier) fr. L. calendue, kalendae, calends. See Calends.

calender.etymology: F. calandre, LL. calendra, corrupted fr. L. cylindrus a cylinder, Gr. Cylinider.

calf.etymology: OE. calf, kelf, AS. cealf; akin to D. kalf, G. kalb, Icel. kalfr, Sw. kalf, Dan. kalv, Goth. kalbo; cf. Skr. garbha fetus, young, Gr. grabh to seize, conceive, Ir. colpa, colpach, a calf. *222.

caliber.etymology: F. calibre, perh. fr. L. qualibra of what pound, of what weight; hence, of what size, applied first to a ball or bullet; cf. also Ar. qalib model, mold. Cf. Calipers, Calivere.

calibre.etymology: F. calibre, perh. fr. L. qualibra of what pound, of what weight; hence, of what size, applied first to a ball or bullet; cf. also Ar. qalib model, mold. Cf. Calipers, Calivere.

calico.etymology: So called because first imported from Calicut, in the East Indies: cf. F. calicot.

caliph.etymology: OE. caliphe, califfe, F. calife (cf. Sp. califa), fr. Ar. khalifan successor, fr. khalafa to succed.

calk.etymology: Either corrupted fr. F. calfater (cf. Pg. calafetar, Sp. calafetear), fr. Ar. qalafa to fill up crevices with the fibers of palm tree or moss; or fr. OE. cauken to tred, through the French fr. L. calcare, fr. calx heel. Cf. Calk to copy, Inculcate.

call.etymology: OE. callen, AS. ceallin; akin to Icel & Sw. kalla, Dan. kalde, D. kallen to talk, prate, Gr. gar to praise. Cf. Garrulous.

callous.etymology: L. callosus callous hard, fr. callum, callus, callous skin: cf. F. calleux.

callow.etymology: OE. calewe, calu, bald, AS. calu; akin to D. kaal, OHG. chalo, G. Kuhl; cf. L. calvus.

calm.etymology: OE. calme, F. calme, fr. It. or Sp. calma (cf. Pg. calma heat), prob. fr. LL. cauma heat, fr. Gr. Caustic

caloric.etymology: L. calor heat; cf. F. calorique.

calorific.etymology: L. calorificus; calor heat + facere to make; cf. F. calorifique.

calorimeter.etymology: L. calor heat + -meter; cf. F. calorimètre.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

caltrop.etymology: OE. calketrappe, calletrappe, caltor (in both senses), fr. AS. collræppe, calcetreppe, sort of thistle; cf. F. chaussetrape star thistle, trap, It. calcatreppo, calcatreppolo, star thistle. Perh. from L. calx heel + the same word as E. trap. See 1st Trap.

calumet.etymology: F. calumet, fr. L. calamus reed. See Halm, and cf. Shawm.

calumniate.etymology: L. calumniatus, p. p. of calumniari. See Calumny, and cf. Challenge, v. t.

calumny.etymology: L. calumnia, fr. calvi to devise tricks, deceive; cf. F. calomnie. Cf. Challenge, n.

calvary.etymology: L. calvaria a bare skull, fr. calva the scalp without hair. fr. calvus bald; cf. F. calvaire.

calx.etymology: L. Calx, calcis. limestone; cf. Gr. carraic rock Gael. carraig, W. careg, stone. Cf. Chalk.

calycle.etymology: L.calyculus small flower bud, calyx, dim. of calyx. See Calyx, and cf. Calicle.

calypso.etymology: The Latinized Greek name of a beautiful nymph.

calyx.etymology: L. calyx, -ycis, fr. Gr. Chalice Helmet.

cam.etymology: Dan. kam comb, ridge; or cf. W. Gael., and Ir., cam bet. See 1st Come.

camail.etymology: F. camail (cf. It. camaglio), fr. L. caput head + source of E. mail.

camber.etymology: Of. cambre bent, curved; akin to F. cambrer to vault, to bend, fr. L. camerare to arch over, fr. camera vault, arch. See Chamber, and cf. Camerate.

cambial.etymology: LL. cambialis, fr. cambiars. See Change.

cambium.etymology: LL. cambium exchange, fr. L. cambire to exchange. It was supposed that cambium was sap changing into wood.

cambric.etymology: OE. camerike, fr. Cambrai (Flemish Kamerik), a city of France (formerly of Flanders), where it was first made.

camel.etymology: Oe. camel, chamel, OF. camel, chamel, F. chameau L. camelus, fr. Gr. gamal, Ar. jamal. Cf. As. camel, fr. L. camelus.

camellia.etymology: NL.; -- named after Kamel, a Jesuit who is said to have brought it from the East.

camelopard.etymology: LL. camelopardus, L. camelopardalus, camelopardalis, fr. Gr. camélopard. The camelopard has a neck and head like a camel, and is spotted like a pard. See Camel, and Pard.

cameo.etymology: It cammeo; akin to F. camée, camaïeu, Sp. camafeo, LL. camaeus, camahutus; of unknown origin.

camera.etymology: L. vault, arch, LL., chamber. See Chamber.

camlet.etymology: F. camelot (akin to Sp. camelote, chamelote, It. cambellbito, ciambellotto, LL. camelotum, camelinum, fr. Ar. khamlat camlet, fr. kaml pile, plush. The word was early confused with camel, camel's hair also being used in making it. Cf. Calamanco

camomile.etymology: LL. camonilla, corrupted fr. Gr. Humble, and Melon.

camp.etymology: F. camp, It. campo, fr. L. campus plant, fleld; akin to Gr. Campaing, Champ, n.

campaign.etymology: F. campagne, It. campagna, fr. L. Campania the level country about Naples, fr. campus field. See Camp, and cf. Champaign, Champagne.

campanile.etymology: It. campanile bell tower, steeple, fr. It. & LL. campana bell.

campanula.etymology: LL. campanula a little bell; dim. of campana bell.

camphor.etymology: OE. camfere, F. camphre (cf. It. camfara, Sp. camfara, alcanfor, LL. camfora, camphara, NGr. kafur, prob. fr. Skr. karpura.

can.etymology: OE. & AS. canne; akin to D. Kan, G. Kanne, OHG. channa, Sw. Kanna, Dan. kande.

canal.etymology: F. canal, from L. canalis canal, channel; prob. from a root signifying "to cut"; cf. D. kanaal, fr. the French. Cf. Channel, Kennel gutter.

canaliculate.etymology: L. canaliculatus channeled, fr. canaliculus, dim. of canalis. See Canal.

canape.etymology: F., orig. a couch with mosquito curtains. See Canopy.

canary.etymology: F. Canarie, L. Canaria insula one of the Canary islands, said to be so called from its large dogs, fr. canis dog.

cancel.etymology: L. cancellare to make like a lattice, to strike or cross out (cf. Fr. canceller, OF. canceler) fr. cancelli lattice, crossbars, dim. of cancer lattice; cf. Gr. Chancel.

cancellate.etymology: L. cancellatus, p. p. of cancellare, See Cancel, v. t.

cancellous.etymology: Cf. L. cancellosus covered with bars.

cancer.etymology: L. cancer, cancri, crab, ulcer, a sign of the zodiac; akin to Gr. karka crab, and prob. Skr. karkara hard, the crab being named from its hard shell. Cf. Canner, Chancre.

candelabrum.etymology: L., fr. candela candle. See candle.

candent.etymology: L. candens, p. pr. of candëre to glitter. See Candid.

candescent.etymology: L. candescens, -entis, p. pr. of candescere, v. incho. fr. candere to shine.

candid.etymology: F. candide (cf. It. candido), L. candidus white, fr. candëre to be of a glowing white; akin to accend, incend, to set on fire, Skr. chand to shane. Cf. Candle, Incense.

candidate.etymology: L. Candidatus, n. (because candidates for office in Rome were clothed in a white toga.) fr. candidatus clothed in white, fr. candiduslittering, white: cf. F. candidat.

candle.etymology: OE. candel, candel, AS, candel, fr. L. candela a (white) light made of wax or tallow, fr. candëre to be white. See Candid, and cf. Chandler, Cannel, Kindle.

candlemas.etymology: AS. candelmæsse, candel candle _ mæsse mass.

candlestick.etymology: AS. candel-sticca; candel candle + sticca stick.

candor.etymology: L. candor, fr. candëre; cf. F. candeur. See candid.

candy.etymology: F. candir (cf. It. candire, Sp. azúcar cande or candi), fr. Ar. & Pers. qand, fr. Skr. Khan\'c8da piece, sugar in pieces or lumps, fr. khan\'c8, khad to break.

cane.etymology: OE. cane, canne, OF. cane, F. canne, L. canna, fr. Gr. qaneh reed. Cf. Canister, canon, 1st Cannon.

canella.etymology: LL. (OE. canel, canelle, cinnamon, fr. F. cannelle), Dim. of L. canna a reed. Canella is so called from the shape of the rolls of prepared bark. See Cane.

canescent.etymology: L. canescens, p. pr. of canescere, v. inchoative of canere to be white.

cangue.etymology: F. cangue, fr. Pg. canga yoke.

canicula.etymology: L. canicula, lit., a little dog, a dim of canis dog; cf. F. canicule.

canine.etymology: L. caninus, fr. canis dog: cf. F. canin. See Hound.

canister.etymology: L. canistrum a basket woven from reeds Gr. canistre. See Cane, and Canaster.

canker.etymology: OE. canker, cancre, AS. cancer (akin to D. kanker, OHG chanchar.), fr. L. cancer a cancer; or if a native word, cf. Gr. cancre, F. chancere, fr. L. cancer. See cancer, and cf. Chancre.

cannibal.etymology: Cf. F. cannibale. Columbus, in a letter to the Spanish monarchs written in Oct., 1498, mentions that the people of Hayti lived in great fear of the Caribales (equivalent to E. Caribbees.), the inhabitants of the smaller Antilles; which form of the name was afterward changed into NL. Canibales, in order to express more forcibly their character by a word intelligible through a Latin root "propter rabiem caninam anthropophagorum gentis." The Caribbees call themselves, in their own language. Calinago, Carinago, Calliponam, and, abbreviated, Calina, signifying a brave, from which Columbus formed his Caribales.

roots.meaning: A diminutive suffix; as, manikin; lambkin.

cannon.etymology: F. cannon, fr. L. canna reed, pipe, tube. See Cane.

cannula.etymology: L. cannula a small tube of dim. of canna a reed, tube.

canny.etymology: Cf. Icel. kenn skilled, learned, or E. canny. Cf. Kenn.

canon.etymology: OE. canon, canoun, AS. canon rule (cf. F. canon, LL. canon, and, for sense 7, F. chanoine, LL. canonicus), fr. L. canon a measuring line, rule, model, fr. Gr. Cane, and cf. Canonical.

canonic.etymology: L. cannonicus, LL. canonicalis, fr. L. canon: cf. F. canonique. See canon.

canonize.etymology: F. canoniser or LL. canonizare, fr. L. canon.. See Canon.

canopy.etymology: Oe. canopie, F. canopésofa, Of canopée, canopeu, canopieu, canopy, vail, pavilion (cf. It. canepècanopy, sofa), LL. canopeum a bed with mosquito curtains, fr. Gr. Cone, and Optic.

canorous.etymology: L. canorus, from nor melody, fr. canere to sing.

cant.etymology: OF., edge, angle, prof. from L. canthus the iron ring round a carriage wheel, a wheel, Gr. cant the stake or tire of a wheel. Cf. Canthus, Canton, Cantle.

cantaloupe.etymology: F. cantaloup, It. cantalupo, so called from the caste of Cantalupo, in the Marca d'Ancona, in Italy, where they were first grown in Europe, from seed said to have been imported from Armenia.

cantata.etymology: It., fr. cantare to sing, fr. L. cantare intens of canere to sing.

canteen.etymology: F. cantine bottle case, canteen (cf. Sp. & It. cantina cellar, bottle case), either contr. fr. It. canovettina, dim. of canova cellar, or, more likely, fr. OF. cant. corner, It. & Sp. canto. See 1st Cant.

canter.etymology: An abbreviation of Caner bury. See Canterbury gallop, under Canterbury.

canticle.etymology: L. canticulum a little song, dim. of canticum song, fr. cantus a singing, fr. coner to sing. See Chant.

cantillate.etymology: L. cantillatus, p. p. of cantillare to sing low, dim. of cantare. See Cantata.

cantle.etymology: OF. cantel, chantel, corner, side, piece, F. chanteau a piece cut from a larger piece, dim. of OF. cant edge, corner. See 1st Cant.

canto.etymology: It. canto, fr. L. cantus singing, song. See Chant.

canton.etymology: F. canton, augm. of OF. cant edge, corner. See 1st Cant.

cantor.etymology: L., a singer, fr. caner to sing.

canvas.etymology: OE. canvas, canevas, F. canevas, LL. canabacius hempen cloth, canvas, L. cannabis hemp, fr. G. Hemp.

canvass.etymology: OF. Canabasser to examine curiously, to search or sift out; properly, to sift through canvas. See Canvas, n.

canyon.etymology: Sp., a tube or hollow, fr. caña reed, fr. L. canna. See Cane.

caoutchouc.etymology: F. caoutchouc, from the South American name.

cap.etymology: OE. cappe, AS. cæppe, cap, cape, hood, fr. LL, cappa, capa; perhaps of Iberian origin, as Isidorus of Seville mentions it first: "Capa, quia quasi totum capiat hominem; it. capitis ornamentum." See 3d Cape, and cf. 1st Cope.

capable.etymology: F. capable, LL. capabilis capacious, capable, fr. L. caper to take, contain. See Heave.

capacious.etymology: L. capaz, -acis, fr. capere to take. See Heave.

capacity.etymology: L. capacitus, fr. capax, capacis; fr. F. capacité. See Capacious.

caparison.etymology: F. capara, fr. Sp. caparazon a cover for a saddle, coach, etc.; capa cloak, cover (fr. LL. capa, cf. LL. caparo also fr. capa) + the term. azon. See Cap.

cape.etymology: F. cap, fr. It. capo head, cape, fr. L. caput heat, end, point. See Chief.

capella.etymology: L., a little goet, dim. of caper a goat.

caper.etymology: From older capreoll to caper, cf. F. se cabrer to prance; all ultimately fr. L. caper, capra, goat. See Capriole.

capillary.etymology: L. capillaris, fr. capillus hair. Cf. Capillaire.

capital.etymology: F. capital, L. capitalis capital (in senses 1 & 2), fr. caput head. See Chief, and cf. Capital, n.

capitation.etymology: L. capitatio a poll tax, fr. caput head; cf. F. capitation.

capitol.etymology: L. capitolium, fr. caput head: cf. F. capitole. See Chief.

capitular.etymology: LL. capitulare, capitularium, fr. L. capitulum a small head, a chapter, dim. of capit head, chapter.

capitulate.etymology: LL. capitulatus, p. p. of capitulare to capitulate: cf. F. capituler. See Capitular, n.

capon.etymology: OE. capon, chapoun, AS. cap (cf. F. chapon), L. capo, fr. Gr. skopiti to casrate. CF. Comma.

capote.etymology: Sp. capote (cf. F. capote.), fr. LL. capa cape, cloak. See Cap.

caprice.etymology: F. caprice, It. capriccio, caprice (perh. orig. a fantastical goat leap), fr. L. caper, capra, goat. Cf Capriole, Cab, Caper, v. i.

capricorn.etymology: L. capricornus; caper goat + cornu horn: cf. F. capricorne.

capriole.etymology: F. capriole, cabriole, It. capriola, fr. L. caper goat. Cf. Caper, v. i. Cabriole, Caprice, Cheveril.

capsicum.etymology: NL., fr. L. capsa box, chest.

capsize.etymology: Cf. Sp. cabecear to nod, pitch, capuzar, chapuzar, to sink (a vessel) by the head; both fr. L. caput head.

capstan.etymology: F. cabestan, fr. Sp. cabestrante, cabrestante, fr. cabestrar to bind with a halter, fr. cabestrohalter, fr. L. capistrum halter, fr. capere to hold (see Capacious); or perh. the Spanish is fr. L. caper goat + stans, p. pr. of stare to stand; cf. F. chèvre she-goat, also a machine for raising heavy weights.

capsule.etymology: L. capsula a little box or chest, fr. capsa chest, case, fr. capere to take, contain: cf. F. capsule.

captain.etymology: OE. capitain, captain, OF. capitain, F. capitaine (cf. Sp. capitan, It. capitano), LL. capitaneus, capitanus, fr. L. caput the head. See under Chief, and cf. Chieftain.

caption.etymology: L. captio, fr. caper to take. In senses 3 and 4, perhaps confounded in meaning with L. caput a head. See Capacious.

captious.etymology: F. captieux, L. captiosus. See Caption.

captivate.etymology: L. captivatus, p. p. of captivare to capture, fr. captivus captive. See Captive.

captive.etymology: L. captivus, fr. capere to take: cf. F. captif. See Caitiff.

captor.etymology: L., a cather (of animals), fr. caper to take.

capture.etymology: L. capture, fr. caper to take: cf. F. capture. See Caitiff, and cf. aptive.

capuchin.etymology: F. capucin a monk who wears a cowl, fr. It. cappuccio hood. See Capoch.

capybara.etymology: Sp. capibara, fr. the native name.

car.etymology: OF. car, char, F. cahr, fr. L. carrus, Wagon: a Celtic word; cf. W. car, Armor. karr, Ir. & Gael. carr. cf. Chariot.

caracal.etymology: F. caracal, fr. Turk garahgootag; garah black + goofag ear.

carack.etymology: F. caraque (cf. Sp. & Pg. carraca, It. caracca.), LL. carraca, fr. L. carrus wagon; or perh. fr. Ar. qorqur (pl. qaraqir) a carack.

caracole.etymology: F. caracole, caracol, fr. Sp. caracol snail, winding staircase, a wheeling about.

caramel.etymology: F. caramel (cf. Sp. caramelo), LL. canna mellis, cannamella, canamella, calamellus mellitus, sugar cane, from or confused with L. canna reed + mel, mellis, honey. See Cane.

carat.etymology: F. carat (cf. It. carato, OPg. quirate, Pg. & Sp. quilate), Ar. q bean or pea shell, a weight of four grins, a carat, fr. Gr. Horn.

caravan.etymology: F. caravane (cf. Sp. caravana), fr. Per. karmwan a caravan (in sense 1). Cf. Van a wagon.

caravansary.etymology: F. caravansérai, fr. Per. karwansara\'8b; karwan caravan + -sara\'8b palace, large house, inn.

caraway.etymology: F. carvi (cf. Sp. carvi and al-caravea, al- carahueya, Pg. al-caravia) fr. Ar. karawi\'befr. Gr. caraum.

roots.meaning: All; wholly; completely; as, almighty,almost. (b) Etym: [L. ad.]

A suffix used to denote: (a) The nonmetallic, or negative, element or radical in a binary compound; as, oxide, sulphide, chloride. (b) A compound which is an anhydride; as, glycolide, phthalide. (c) Any one of a series of derivatives; as, indogenide, glucoside, etc.

carbine.etymology: F. carbine, OF. calabrin carabineer (cf. Ot. calabrina a policeman), fr. OF & Pr. calabre, OF. cable, chable, an engine of war used in besieging, fr. LL. chadabula, cabulus, a kind of projectile machine, fr. Gr. Parable.

carbonado.etymology: Cf. F. carbonnade, It. carbonata, Sp. carbonada, from L. carbo coal.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying bearing, producing, yielding; as, auriferous, yielding gold; chyliferous, producing chyle.
A suffix used as a characteristic termination of chemical radicals; as in ethyl, carbonyl, hydroxyl, etc.
A suffix used as a characteristic termination of chemical radicals; as in ethyl, carbonyl, hydroxyl, etc.

carboy.etymology: Cf. Ir. & Gael carb basket; or Pers qurabah a sort of bottle.

carbuncle.etymology: L. carbunculus a little coal, a bright kind of precious stone, a kind of tumor, dim. of carbo coal: cf. F. carboncle. See Carbon.

carcajou.etymology: Probably a Canadian French corruption of an Indian name of the wolverene.

carcass.etymology: F. carcasse, fr. It. carcassa, fr. L. caro flesh + capsa chest, box, case. Cf. Carnal, Case a sheath.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote a morbid condition of some part, usually some kind of tumor; as in fibroma, glaucoma.

card.etymology: F. carte, fr. L. charta paper, Gr. Chart.

cardinal.etymology: L. cardinalis, fr. cardo the hing of a door, that on which a thing turns or depends: cf. F. cardinal.

roots.meaning: A suffix indicating something drawn or written, a drawing, writing; -- as, monogram, telegram, chronogram.
A suffix signifying something written, a writing; also, a writer; as autograph, crystograph, telegraph, photograph.

carditis.etymology: NL., fr. Gr. -itis: cf. F. cardile.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.

cardoon.etymology: F. cardon. The same word as F. cardon thistle, fr. L. carduus, cardus, LL. cardo. See 3d Card.

care.etymology: AS. caru, cearu; akin to OS. kara sorrow Goth. kara lament, and to Gr. . Not akin to cure. Cf. Chary.

careen.etymology: OF. cariner, F. caréner, fr. OF. carène, the bottom of a ship, keel, fr. L. carina.

career.etymology: F. carrière race course, high road, street, fr. L. carrus wagon. See Car.

caress.etymology: F. caresse, It. carezza, LL. caritia dearness, fr. L. carus dear. See Charity.

caret.etymology: L. caret there is wanting, fr. carere to want.

cargo.etymology: Sp. cargo, carga, burden, load, from cargar to load, from cargar to load, charge, See Charge.

caricature.etymology: It. caricatura, fr. caricare to charge, overload, exaggerate. See Charge, v. t.

carillon.etymology: F. carillon a chime of bells, originally consisting of four bells, as if fr.. (assumed) L. quadrilio, fr. quatuer four.

cark.etymology: OE. cark, fr. a dialectic form of F. charge; cf. W. carc anxiety, care, Arm karg charge, burden. See Charge, and cf. Cargo.

carminative.etymology: NL. carminativus (carminare to card hence to cleanse, fr. carmen a card for freeing wool or flax from the coarser parts, and from extraneous matter: cf. F. carminatif.

carmine.etymology: F. carmin (cf. Sp. carmin, It. carminio), contr. from LL. carmesinus purple color. See Crimson.

carnage.etymology: F. carnage, LL. carnaticum tribute of animals, flesh of animals, fr. L. caro, carnis, flesh. See Carnal.

carnal.etymology: L. carnalis, fr. caro, carnis, flesh; akin to Gr. kravya; cf. F. charnel, Of. also carnel. Cf. Charnel.

carnallite.etymology: G. carnallit, fr. Von Carnall, a Prussian.

carnassial.etymology: Cf. F. carnassier carnivorous, and L. caro, carnis, flesh.

carnation.etymology: F. carnation the flesh tints in a painting, It carnagione, fr. L. carnatio fleshiness, fr. caro, carnis, flesh. See Carnal.

carnelian.etymology: For carnelian; influenced by L. carneus fleshy, of flesh, because of its flesh red color. See Cornellan.

carnify.etymology: LL. carnificare, fr. L.o, carnis, flesh + facere to make: cf. F. carnifier.

carnival.etymology: It. carnevale, prob. for older carnelevale, prop., the putting away of meat; fr. L. caro, carnis, flesh _ levare to take away, lift up, fr. levis light.

carnivora.etymology: NL., neut. pl. from L. carnivorus. See Carnivorous.

carnivorous.etymology: L. carnivorus; caro, carnis, flesh + varare to devour.

carob.etymology: Cf. F. caroube fruit of the carob tree, Sp. garrobo, al-garrobo, carob tree, fr. Ar. kharrub, Per. Kharnub. Cf. Clgaroba.

caroche.etymology: OF. carrache, F. carrose from It. carrocio, carrozza, fr. carro, L. carus. See Car.

carol.etymology: OF. carole a kind of dance wherein many dance together, fr. caroler to dance; perh. from Celtic; cf. Armor. koroll, n., korolla, korolli, v., Ir. car music, turn, circular motion, also L. choraula a flute player, charus a dance, chorus, choir.

caroline.etymology: F. carin; cf. It. carlino; -- so called from Carlo (Charles) VI. of Naples.

carom.etymology: Prob. corrupted fr. F. carumboler to carom, carambolage a carom, carambole the red ball in billiards.

carotid.etymology: Gr. carotide. The early Greeks believed that these arteries in some way caused drowsiness.

carousal.etymology: See Carouse, but also cf. F. carrousel tilt.

carouse.etymology: F. carrousse, earlier carous, fr. G. garaus finishing stroke, the emptying of the cup in drinking a health; gar entirely + aus out. See Yare, and Out.

carp.etymology: OE. carpen to say, speak; from Scand. (cf. Icel. karpa to boast), but influenced later by L. carpere to pluck, calumniate.

carpenter.etymology: OF. carpentier, F. charpentier, LL. carpentarius, fr. L. carpentum wagon, carriage.

carpentry.etymology: F. charpenterie, OF. also carpenterie. See Carpenter.

carpet.etymology: OF. carpite rug, soft of cloth, F. carpette coarse packing cloth, rug (cf. It. carpita rug, blanket), LL. carpeta, carpita, woolly cloths, fr. L. carpere to pluck, to card (wool); cf. Gr. Harvest.

carriage.etymology: OF. cariage luggage, carriage, chariage carriage, cart, baggage, F. charriage, cartage, wagoning, fr. OF. carier, charier, F. charrier, to cart. See Carry.

carrion.etymology: OE. caroyne, OF. caroigne, F. charogne, LL. caronia, fr. L. caro flesh Cf. Crone, Crony.

carry.etymology: OF. carier, charier, F. carrier, to cart, from OF. car, char, F. car, car. See Car.

cart.etymology: AS. cræt; cf. W. cart, Ir. & Gael. cairt, or Icel. kartr. Cf. Car.

cartel.etymology: F., fr. LL. cartellus a little paper, dim. fr. L. charta. See 1st Card.

cartesian.etymology: From Renatus Cartesius, Latinized from of René Descartes: cf. F. cartésien.

carthusian.etymology: LL. Cartusianus, Cartusiensis, from the town of Chartreuse, in France.

cartilaginification.etymology: L. cartilago, -laginis, cartilage + facere to make.

cartography.etymology: Cf. F. cartographie. See Card, and - graphy.

cartoon.etymology: F. carton (cf. It. cartons pasteboard, cartoon.); fr. L. charta. See 1st card.

cartouch.etymology: F. cartouche, It. cartuccia, cartoccio, cornet, cartouch, fr. L. charta paper. See 1st Card, and cf. Cartridge.

cartridge.etymology: Formerlly cartrage, corrupted fr. F. cartouche. See Cartouch.

caruncle.etymology: L. caruncula a little piece of flesh, dim. of caro flesh.

caruncula.etymology: L. caruncula a little piece of flesh, dim. of caro flesh.

carve.etymology: AS. ceorfan to cut, carve; akin to D. kerven, G. kerben, Dan. karve, Sw. karfva, and to Gr. -graphy. Cf. Graphic.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting the art of writing or describing; also, the writing or description itself; a treatise; as, calligraphy, biography, geography.

cascabel.etymology: Sp. cascabel a little bell, also (fr. the shape), a knob at the breech end of a cannon.

cascade.etymology: F. cascade, fr. It. cascata, fr. cascare to ball.

cascarilla.etymology: Sp., small thin bark, Peruvian bark, dim. of cáscara bark.

case.etymology: OF. casse, F. caisse (cf. It. cassa), fr. L. capsa chest, box, case, fr. caper to take, hold See Capacious, and cf. 4th Chase, Cash, Enchase, 3d Sash.

casein.etymology: Cf. F. caséine, fr. L. caseur cheese. Cf. Cheese.

casement.etymology: Shortened fr. encasement. See Incase 1st Case, and cf. Incasement.

cash.etymology: F. caisse case, box, cash box, cash. See Case a box.

cashew.etymology: F. acajou, for cajou, prob. from Malay kayu tree; cf. Pg. acaju, cf. Acajou.

cashier.etymology: F. caissier, fr. caisse. See Cash.

casino.etymology: It. casino, dim. of casa house, fr. L. casa cottage. Cf. Cassing.

cask.etymology: Sp. casco potsherd, skull, helmet, prob. fr. cascar to break, fr. L. Quassure to break. Cf. Casque, Cass.

casket.etymology: Cf. F. casquet, dim. of casque belmet, fr. Sp. casco.

casque.etymology: F. casque, fr. Sp. casco See Cask.

cassava.etymology: F. cassave, Sp. cazabe, fr. kasabi, in the language of Hayti.

casserole.etymology: F. a saucepan, dim. from casse a basin.

cassette.etymology: F., prop., a casket, dim. of casse a case. See lst Case.

cassia.etymology: L. cassia and casia, Gr. qetsi\'beh, fr. qatsa' to cut off, to peel off.

cassino.etymology: It. casino a small house, a gaming house. See asing.

cassius.etymology: From the name of the discoverer, A. Cassius, a German physician of the 17th centry.

cassock.etymology: F. casaque, fr. It. casacca, perh. fr. L. casa cottage, in It., house; or of Slavic origin.

cast.etymology: Cf. Dan. kastw, Icel. & Sw. kasta; perh. akin to L. gerer to bear, carry. E. Jest.

castanets.etymology: F. castagnettes, Sp. castañetas, fr. L. castanea (Sp. castaña) a chestnut. So named from the resemblance to two chestnuts, or because chestnuts were first used for castanets. See Chestnut.

caste.etymology: Pg. casta race, lineage, fr. L. castus pure, chaste: cf. F. caste, of same origin.

castellated.etymology: LL. castellatus, fr. castellare. See Castle.

castigate.etymology: L. castigatus, p. p. of castigare to correct, punish; castus pure, chaste + agere to move, drive. See Caste, and cf. Chasten.

castilian.etymology: Sp. castellano, from Castila, NL. Castilia, Castella. Castile, which received its name from the castles erected on the frontiers as a barrier against the Moors.

castle.etymology: AS. castel, fr. L. castellum, dim. of castrum a fortified place, castle.

castrate.etymology: L. castrarus, p; p. of castrare to castrate, asin to Skr. çastra knife.

castrato.etymology: L., properly p. p. of castrare. See Castrate.

casual.etymology: OE. casuel, F. casuel, fr. L. casualis, fr. casus fall, accident, fr. cadere to fall. See Case.

casuarina.etymology: NL., supposed to be named from the resemblance of the twigs to the feathers of the cassowary, of the genus Casuarius.

casuist.etymology: L. casus fall, case; cf. F. casuiste. See Casual.

cat.etymology: AS. cat; akin to D. & Dan. kat, Sw. kett, Icel. köttr, G. katze, kater, Ir. Cat, W. cath, Armor. kaz, LL. catus, Bisc. catua, NGr cot, Turk. kedi, Ar. qitt; of unknown origin. CF. Ketten.

catafalque.etymology: F., fr. It. catafalco, scaffold, funeral canopy; of uncertain origin; cf. Sp. catafalso, cadahalso, cadalso, Pr. casafalc, OF. chafaut. Cf. Scaffold.

catalpa.etymology: From the language of the Indians of Carolina, where Catesby discovered this tree in the year 1726.

catamount.etymology: Cat + mount; cf. Sp. gato mentes mountain cat.

catch.etymology: OE. cacchen, OF. cachier, dialectic form of chacier to hunt, F. chasser, fr. (assumend) LL. captiare, for L. capture, V. intens. of capere to take, catch. See Capacious, and cf. Chase, Case a box.

catechism.etymology: L. catechismus, fr. Gr. See Catechise.

catenary.etymology: L. catenarius, fr. catena a chain. See Chain.

catenate.etymology: L. catenatus, p. p. of catenare, fr. catena chain. See Chain.

catenulate.etymology: L. catenuia, dim. of catena chain.

cater.etymology: OE. catour purchaser, caterer, OF. acator, fr. acater, F. acheter, to buy, provide, fr. LL. accaptare; L. ad + captare to strive, to seize, intens, of capere to take, seize. Cf. Acater, Capacious.

caterpillar.etymology: OE. catyrpel, corrupted fr. OF. chatepelouse, or cate pelue, fr. chate, F. chatte, she-cat, fem. of chat, L. catus + L. pilosus hairy, or F. pelu hairy, fr. L. pilus hair. See Cat, and Pile hair.

caterwaul.etymology: Cat + waul, wawl, to cry as a cat.

cathedral.etymology: LL. cathedralis (sc. ecclesia): cf. F. cathédrale. See Cathedra.

catholic.etymology: L. catholicus, Gr. solid: cf. F. catholique.

roots.meaning: A diminutive suffix; as, manikin; lambkin.
A suffix used to from present participles; as, singing, playing.

catsup.etymology: Probably of East Indian origin, because it was originally a kind of East Indian pickles.

cattle.etymology: OE. calet, chatel, goods, property, OF. catel, chatel, LL. captale, capitale, goods, property, esp. cattle, fr. L. capitals relating to the head, chief; because in early ages beasts constituted the chief part of a man's property. See Capital, and cf. Chattel.

caucus.etymology: Etymology uncertain. Mr. J. H. Trumbull finds the origin of caucus in the N. A. Indian word cawcawwassough or caú cau- as'u one who urges or pushes on, a promoter. See citation for an early use of the word caucus.

caul.etymology: OE. calle, kelle, prob. fr. F. cale; cf. Ir. calla a veil.

caulescent.etymology: L. caulis stalk, stem: cf. F. caulescent.

cauliflower.etymology: F. choufleur, modified by E. Cole. L. caulis, and by E. flower; F. chou cabbage is fr. L. caulis stalk, cabbage, and fleur flower is fr. L. flos flower. See Cole, and Flower.

causative.etymology: L. causativus pertaining to a lawsuit (causa), but in the English sense from E. cause.

cause.etymology: F. cause, fr. L. causa. Cf. Cause, v., Kickshaw.

causeway.etymology: OE. cauci, cauchie, OF. cauchie, F. chaussée, from LL. (via) calciata, fr calciare to make a road, either fr. L. calx lime, hence, to pave with limestone (cf. E. chalk), or from L. calceus shoe, from calx heel, hence, to shoe, pave, or wear by treading.

cauterize.etymology: L. cauterizare, Gr. cautérised.. See cauter.

caution.etymology: F. caution a security, L. cautio, fr. cavere (For scavere) to be on one's guard, to take care (orig.) to be on the watch, see; akin to E. show.

cautious.etymology: Cf. L. cautus, fr. caver. See Caution.

cavalcade.etymology: F. cavalcade, fr. It. cavalcata, fr. cavalcare to go on horseback, fr. LL. caballicare, fr. L. caballus an inferior horse, Gr. Cavalier, Cavalry.

cavalier.etymology: F. cavalier, It. cavaliere, LL. caballarius, fr. L. caballus. See Cavalcade, and cf. Cavallier, Caballine.

cavalry.etymology: F. cavalerie, fr. It. cavalleria. See Cavalier, and cf. chivalry.

cave.etymology: F. cave, L. cavus hollow, whence cavea cavity. Cf. Cage.

caveat.etymology: L. caved let him beware, pres. subj. of cavere to be on one's guard to, beware.

cavern.etymology: L. caverna, fr. cavus hollow: cf. F. caverne.

cavetto.etymology: It. cavetto, fr. cavo hollow, L. cavus.

caviar.etymology: F. caviar, fr. It. caviale, fr. Turk. Havi\'ber.

caviare.etymology: F. caviar, fr. It. caviale, fr. Turk. Havi\'ber.

cavil.etymology: L. cavillari to practice jesting, to censure, fr. cavilla bantering jests, sophistry: cf. OF. caviller.

cavity.etymology: L. cavus hollow: cf. F. cavité.

cavy.etymology: NL. cavia, fr. Brazilian cabiai: cf. F. cabiai.

cayenne.etymology: From Cayenne, a town and island in French Guiana, South America.

cayman.etymology: From the language of Guiana: cf. Sp. caiman.

cazique.etymology: Sp. Cacique, fr. the language of Hayti.

cease.etymology: OE. cessen, cesen, F. cesser, fr. L. cessare, v. intemsive fr. cedere to withdraw. See Cede , and cf. Cessation.

cecity.etymology: L. caecitas, fr. caecus blind: cf. F. cécité.

cede.etymology: L. cedere to withdraw, yield; akin to cadere to fall, and to E. chance; cf. F. céder.

cedilla.etymology: Sp. cedilla, cf. F. cédille; dim. of zeta, the Gr. name of the letter z, because this letter was formerly written after the c, to give it the sound of s.

celandine.etymology: OE. celidoine, OF. celidoine, F. chélidoine, fr. L. chelidonia (sc. herba), fr. chelidonius pertaining to the swallow, Gr. hirundo a swallow.

celebrant.etymology: L. celebrans, p. pr. of celebrare. See Celebrate.

celebrate.etymology: L. celebratus, p. p. of celebrare to frequent, to celebrate, fr. celeber famous.

celerity.etymology: L. celeritas, from celer swiftm speedy: sf. F. célérité.

celery.etymology: F. céleri, cf. Prov. It. seleno, seler; fr. Gr. celery. Cf. Parsley.

celestial.etymology: OF. celestial, celestied, fr. L. caelestic, fr. caelum heaved. See Cell.

celibate.etymology: L. aelibatus, fr. caelebs unmarried, single.

cell.etymology: OF. celle, fr. L. cella; akin to celare to hide, and E. hell, helm, conceal. Cf. Hall.

cellar.etymology: OE. celer, OF. celier, F. celier, fr. L. cellarium a receptacle for food, pantry, fr. cella storeroom. See Cell.

cellular.etymology: L. cellula a little cell: cf. F. cellulaire. See Cellule.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.
A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

celt.etymology: L. Celtae, Gr. Celtiad one that dwells in a covert, an inhabitant of the wood, a Celt, fr. celt covert, shelter, celu to hide.

cement.etymology: OF. cement, ciment, F. ciment, fr. L. caementum a rough, unhewn stone, pieces or chips of marble, from which mortar was made, contr. fr. caedimentum, fr. caedere to cut, prob. akin to scindere to cleave, and to E. shed, v. t.

cementitious.etymology: L. caementitius pertaining to quarry stones. See Cement, n.

cense.etymology: OF. cense, F. cens, L. census. See Census.

censer.etymology: For incenser, fr. OF. encensier, F. encensoir, fr. LL. incensarium, incensorium, fr. L. incensum incense. See Incense, and cf. Incensory.

censor.etymology: L. censor, fr. censere to value, tax.

censorious.etymology: L. censorius pertaining to the censor. See Censor.

censure.etymology: L. censura fr. censere: cf. F. censure. Cf. Censor.

census.etymology: L. census, fr. censere. See Censor.

cent.etymology: F. cent hundred, L. centum. See Hundred.

centenary.etymology: L. centenarius, fr. centum a hundred.

centennial.etymology: L. centum a hundred + annus year.

centesimal.etymology: L. centesimus the hundredth, fr. centum a hundred: cf. F. centésimal.

centigrade.etymology: L. centum a hundred + gradus degree: cf. F. centigrade.

centiliter.etymology: F. centilitre; centi (L. centum) + litre. See Liter.

centilitre.etymology: F. centilitre; centi (L. centum) + litre. See Liter.

centime.etymology: F., fr. L. centesimus. See Centesimal.

centimeter.etymology: F. centimètre; centi- (L. centum) + mètre. See Meter.

centimetre.etymology: F. centimètre; centi- (L. centum) + mètre. See Meter.

centner.etymology: Cf. G. centner a hundred-weight, fr. L. centenarius of a hundred, fr. centum a hundred.

central.etymology: L. centralis, fr. centrum: cf. F. central. See Center.

centrifugal.etymology: L. centrum center + fugere to flee.

centripetal.etymology: L. centrum center + peter to more toward.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

centurion.etymology: L. centurio, fr. centuria; cf. F. centurion. See Century.

century.etymology: L. centuria (in senses 1 & 3), fr. centum a hundred: cf. F. centurie. See Cent.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.

cephalopoda.etymology: NL., gr. Gr. -poda: cf. F. céphalopode.

roots.meaning: A New Latin plural combining form or suffix from Gr. foot; as, hexapoda, myriapoda. See -pod.

cerate.etymology: L. ceratum, ceratm, fr. cera wax.

cere.etymology: L. cera wax: cf. F. cire.

cereal.etymology: L. Cerealis pert. to Ceres, and hence, to agriculture. See Ceres.

cerebral.etymology: L. cerebrum brain; akin to Gr. cérébral. See Cheer.

cerement.etymology: L. cera wax: cf. F. cirement.

ceremonial.etymology: L. caerimonialis: cf. F. cérimonial. See Ceremony.

ceremony.etymology: F. cérémonie, L. caerimonia; perh. akin to E. create and from a root signifying to do or make.

ceres.etymology: L., Ceres, also corn, grain, akin to E. create.

cereus.etymology: L., a wax candle, fr. cera wax. So named from the resemblance of one species to the columnar shape of a wax candle.

cerium.etymology: Named dy Berzelius in 1803 from the asteroid Ceres, then just discovered (1801).

cernuous.etymology: L. cernuus with the face turned toward the earth.

cero.etymology: Corrupt. fr. Sp. sierra saw, sawfish, cero.

certain.etymology: F. certain, fr. (assumed) LL. certanus, fr. L. certus determined, fixed, certain, orig. p. p. of cernere to perceive, decide, determine; akin to Gr. concern, critic, crime, riddle a sieve, rinse, v.

certificate.etymology: F. certificat, fr. LL. certificatus made certain, p. p. of certificare. See tify.

certify.etymology: F. certifier, LL. certificare; L. certus certain + facere to make. See Certain, and cf. Certificate, v. t.

certiorari.etymology: So named from the emphatic word certiorari in the Latin form of the writ, which read certiorar volumus we wish to be certified.

certitude.etymology: LL. certitudo, fr. L. certus: cf. F. certitude. See Certain.

cervical.etymology: L. cervix, -icis, neck: cf. F. cervical.

cervine.etymology: L. cervinus, fr. cervus deer: cf. F. cervin.

cessation.etymology: F. cessation, L. cessatio, fr. cessare. See Cease.

cession.etymology: L. cessio, fr. cedere to give way: cf. F. Cession. See Cede.

chachalaca.etymology: Native name, prob. given in imitation of its cry.

chafe.etymology: OE. chaufen to warm, OF. chaufer, F. chauffer, fr. L. calefacere, calfacere, to make warm; calere to be warm + facere to make. See Caldron.

chaff.etymology: AC. ceaf; akin to D. kaf, G. kaff.

chaffer.etymology: OE. chaffare, cheapfare; AS. ceáp a bargain, price + faru a journey; hence, originally, a going to barain, to market. See Cheap, and Fare.

chagrin.etymology: F., fr. chagrin shagreen, a particular kind of rough and grained leather; also a rough fishskin used for graters and files; hence (Fig.), a gnawing, corroding grief. See Shagreen.

chain.etymology: F. chaîne, fr. L. catena. Cf. Catenate.

chair.etymology: OE. chaiere, chaere, OF. chaiere, chaere, F. chaire pulpit, fr. L. cathedra chair, armchair, a teacher's or professor's chair, Gr. sit. See Sit, and cf. Cathedral, chaise.

chaise.etymology: F. chaise seat, or chair, chaise or carriage, for chaire, from a peculiar Parisian pronunciation. See Chair.

chalcedony.etymology: L. chalcedonius, fr. Gr. calcédoine, OE. calcidoine, casidoyne. Cf. Cassidony.

chalcopyrite.etymology: Gr. pyrite. So named from its color.

chaldron.etymology: OF. chaldron, F. chaudron kettle. The same word as caldron.

chalice.etymology: OR. chalis, calice, OF. chalice, calice, F. calice, fr. L. calix, akin to Gr. helmet. Cf. Calice, Calyx.

chalk.etymology: AS. cealc lime, from L. calx limestone. See Calz, and Cawk.

challenge.etymology: OE. chalenge claim, accusation, challenge, OF. chalenge, chalonge, claim, accusation, contest, fr. L. calumnia false accusation, chicanery. See Calumny.

challis.etymology: F. chaly, challis, a stuff made of goat's hair.

chalybeate.etymology: NL. chalybeatus, fr. chalubeïus. See Chalubean.

chamber.etymology: F. chambre, fr. L. camera vault, arched roof, in LL. chamber, fr. Gr. kmar to be crooked. Cf. Camber, Camera, Comrade.

chamberlain.etymology: OF. chamberlain, chambrelencF. chambellon, OHG. chamerling, chamarlinc, G. kämmerling, kammer chamber (fr. L. camera) + -ling. See Chamber, and -ling.

roots.meaning: A noun suffix, commonly having a diminutive or a depreciatory force; as in duck-ling, dosling, hireling, fosterling, firstling, underling.
A noun suffix, commonly having a diminutive or a depreciatory force; as in duck-ling, dosling, hireling, fosterling, firstling, underling.

chameleon.etymology: L. Chamaeleon, Gr. Humble, and Lion.

chamois.etymology: F. chamois, prob. fr. OG. gamz, G. gemse.

chamomile.etymology: LL. camonilla, corrupted fr. Gr. Humble, and Melon.

champ.etymology: Prob, of Scand. orgin; cf. dial. Sw. kämsa to chew with difficulty, champ; but cf. also OF. champier, champeyer, champoyer, to graze in fields, fr. F. champ field, fr. L. campus. Cf. Camp.

champaign.etymology: OF. champaigne; same word as campagne.

champerty.etymology: F. champart field rent, L. campipars; champ (L. campus) field + part (L. pars) share.

champion.etymology: F. champion, fr. LL.campio, of German origin; cf. OHG. chempho, chemphio, fighter, champf, G. kampf, contest; perh. influenced by L. campus field, taken in the sense of "field of battle."

champleve.etymology: F., p. p. of champlever to engrave. See 3d Champ, Camp, Lever a bar.

chance.etymology: F. chance, OF. cheance, fr. LL. cadentia a allusion to the falling of the dice), fr. L. cadere to fall; akin to Skr. çad to fall, L. cedere to yield, E. cede. Cf. Cadence.

chancel.etymology: OF. chancel, F. chanceau, cancel, fr. L. cancelli lattices, crossbars. (The chancel was formerly inclosed with lattices or crossbars) See Cancel, v. t.

chancellor.etymology: OE. canceler, chaunceler, F. chancelier, LL. cancellarius chancellor, a director of chancery, fr. L. cancelli lattices, crossbars, which surrounded the seat of judgment. See Chancel.

chancery.etymology: F. chancellerie, LL. cancellaria, from L. cancellarius. See Chancellor, and cf. Chancellery.

chandler.etymology: F. chandelier a candlestick, a maker or seller of candles, LL. candelarius chandler, fr. L. candela candle. See Candle, and cf. Chandelier.

change.etymology: F. changer, fr. LL. cambiare, to exchange, barter, L. cambire. Cf. Cambial.

roots.meaning: A noun suffix, commonly having a diminutive or a depreciatory force; as in duck-ling, dosling, hireling, fosterling, firstling, underling.

channel.etymology: OE. chanel, canel, OF. chanel, F. chenel, fr. L. canalis. See Canal.

chant.etymology: F. chanter, fr. L. cantare, intens. of canere to sing. Cf. Cant affected speaking, and see Hen.

chantry.etymology: OF. chanterie, fr. chanter to sing.

chaos.etymology: L. chaos chaos (in senses 1 & 2), Gr. Chasm.

chaparral.etymology: Sp., fr. chaparro an evergeen oak.

chapeau.etymology: F., fr. OF. chapel hat. See Chaplet.

chapel.etymology: OF. chapele, F. chapelle, fr. LL. capella, orig., a short cloak, hood, or cowl; later, a reliquary, sacred vessel, chapel; dim. of cappa, capa, cloak, cape, cope; also, a covering for the head. The chapel where St. Martin's cloak was preserved as a precious relic, itself came to be called capella, whence the name was applied to similar paces of worship, and the guardian of this cloak was called capellanus, or chaplain. See Cap, and cf. Chaplain., Chaplet.

chaperon.etymology: F. chaperon. See Chape, Cape, Cap.

chapiter.etymology: OF. chapitel, F. chapiteau, from L. capitellum, dim. of caput head. Cf. Capital, Chapter.

chaplain.etymology: F. chapelain, fr. LL. capellanus, fr. capella. See Chapel.

chaplet.etymology: F. chapelet, dim. of OF. chapel hat, garland, dim. fr. LL. cappa. See Cap, and cf. Chapelet, Chapeau.

chapman.etymology: AS. ceápman; ceáp trade + man man; akin to D. koopman, Sw. köpman, Dan. kiöpmand, G. kaufmann.f. Chap to cheapen, and see Cheap.

chapter.etymology: OF. chapitre, F. chapitre, fr. L. capitulum, dim. of caput head, the chief person or thing, the principal division of a writing, chapter. See Chief, and cf, Chapiter.

char.etymology: Ir. cear, Gael. ceara, lit., red, blood- colored, fr. cear blood. So named from its red belly.

character.etymology: L., an instrument for marking, character, Gr. caractère.

charade.etymology: F. charade, cf. Pr. charrada long chat, It ciarlare to chat, whence E. charlatan.

charcoal.etymology: See Char, v. t., to burn or to reduce to coal, and Coal.

charge.etymology: OF. chargier, F. charger, fr. LL. carricare, fr. L. carrus wagon. Cf. Cargo, Caricature, Cark, and see Car.

chariot.etymology: F. Chariot, from char car. See Car.

charity.etymology: F. charité fr. L. caritas dearness, high regard, love, from carus dear, costly, loved; asin to Skr. kam to wish, love, cf. Ir. cara a friend, W. caru to love. Cf. Caress.

charlatan.etymology: F. charlatan, fr. It. ciarlatano, fr. ciarlare to chartter, prate; of imitative origin; cf. It. zirlare to whistle like a thrush.

charlock.etymology: AS. cerlic; the latter part perh. fr. AS. leác leek. Cf. Hemlock.

charm.etymology: F. charme, fr. L. carmen song, verse, incantation, for casmen, akin to Skr. çasman, çasa, a laudatory song, from a root signifying to praise, to sing.

charnel.etymology: F. charnel carnal, fleshly, fr. L. carnalis. See Carnal.

charr.etymology: Ir. cear, Gael. ceara, lit., red, blood- colored, fr. cear blood. So named from its red belly.

chart.etymology: A doublet of card: cf. F. charte charter, carte card. See Card, and cf. Charter.

charter.etymology: OF. chartre, F. chartre, charte, fr. L. chartula a little paper, dim. of charta. See Chart, Card.

chartism.etymology: F. charte charter. Cf. Charte, Chart.

chary.etymology: AS. cearig careful, fr. cearu care. See Care.

chase.etymology: OF. chacier, F. chasser, fr. (assumed) LL. captiare, fr. L. captare to strive to seize. See Catch.

chasse.etymology: F., fr. chassé, p. p. of chasser to chase.

chaste.etymology: F. chaste, from L. castus pure, chaste; cf. Gr. to purify.

chasten.etymology: OE. chastien, OF. Chastier, F. Ch, fr. L. castigare to punish, chastise; castus pure + agere to lead, drive. See Chaste, Act, and cf. Castigate, Chastise.

chastise.etymology: OE. chastisen; chastien + ending -isen + modern - ise, ize, L. izare, G. Chasten.

chastity.etymology: F. chasteté, fr. L. castitas, fr. castus. See Chaste.

chasuble.etymology: F. chasuble, LL. casubula, cassibula, casula, a hooded garment, covering the person like a little house; cf. It. casupola, casipola, cottage, dim of L. casa cottage.

chateau.etymology: F. château a castle. See Castle.

chatelaine.etymology: F. châtelaine the wife of a castellan, the mistress of a chateau, a chatelaine chain.

chatoyant.etymology: F., p. pr. of chatoyer to be chatoyant, fr. chat cat.

chattel.etymology: OF. chatel; another form of catel. See Cattle.

chatter.etymology: Of imitative origin. Cf. Chat, v. i. Chitter.

chauvinism.etymology: F. chauvinisme, from Chauvin, a character represented as making grotesque and threatening displays of his attachment to his fallen chief, Napoleon I., in 1815.

cheap.etymology: AS. ceáp bargain, sale, price; akin to D. Koop purchase, G. Kauf, ICel. kaup bargain. Cf. Cheapen, Chapman, Chaffer, Cope, v. i.

cheapen.etymology: OE. cheapien, chepen, to trade, buy, sell, AS. ceápian; akin to D. koopen to buy, G. kaufen, Icel. kaupa, Goth. kaupon to trade. Cf. Chap to bargain.

cheat.etymology: rob. an abbrevation of escheat, lands or tenements that fall to a lord or to the state by forfeiture, or by the death of the tenant without heirs; the meaning being explained by the frauds, real or supposed, that were resorted to in procuring escheats. See Escheat.

check.etymology: OE. chek, OF. eschec, F. échec, a stop, hindrance, orig. check in the game of chess, pl. échecs chess, through AR., fr. Pers. shah king. See Shah, and cf. Checkmate, Chess, Checker.

checkmate.etymology: F. échec et mat, fr. Per. shah mat ceckmate, lit., the king is dead, fr. Ar. mata he died, is dead. The king, when made prisoner, or checkmated, is assumed to be dead, and the game is finished. See Chess.

cheek.etymology: OE. cheke, cheoke, AS. céace, céoce; cf. Goth. kukjan to kiss, D. kaak cheek; perh. akin to E. chew, jaw.

cheer.etymology: OE. chere face, welcome, cheer, OF. chiere, F. chère, fr. LL. cara face, Gr. , L. cerebrum brain, G. hirn, and E. cranium.

cheese.etymology: OE. chese, AS. cese, fr. L. caseus, LL. casius. Cf. Casein.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying bearing, producing, yielding; as, auriferous, yielding gold; chyliferous, producing chyle.

chemise.etymology: F., shirt, fr. LL. camisa, camisia, shirt, thin dress; cf. G. hemd, or Olr. coimumse sort of garment. Cf. Camis.

chemist.etymology: Shortened from alchemist; cf. F. chimiste.

cherish.etymology: F. chérir, fr. cher dear, fr. L. carus. See Caress, Finish.

chert.etymology: Ir. ceart stone, perh. akin to E. crag.

chess.etymology: OE. ches, F. échecs, prop. pl. of échec check. See 1st Check.

chest.etymology: OE. chest, chist, AS. cest, cist, cyst, L. cista, fr. Gr. Cist, Cistern.

chestnut.etymology: For chesten-nut; OE. chestein, chesten, chastein, chestnut, fr. AS. cisten in cistenbeám chestnut tree, influenced by OF. chastaigne, F. châtaigne, both the AS. and the F. words coming from L. castanea a chestnut, Gr. Castanets.

chevalier.etymology: F., fr. LL. caballarius. See Cavaller.

chevron.etymology: F., rafter, chevron, from chévre goat, OF. chevre, fr. L. capra she-goat. See Cheveril.

chevrotain.etymology: F. chevrotin, OF. chevrot little goat, roe, dim. of chevre goat. See Chevron.

chew.etymology: As ceówan, akin to D. kauwen, G. kauen. Cf. Chaw, Jaw.

chicane.etymology: F., prob. earlier meaning a dispute, orig. in the game of mall (F. mail), fr. LGr. chaugan club or bat; or possibly ultimated fr. L. ciccus a trible.

chicken.etymology: AS. cicen, cyceun, dim. of coc cock; akin to LG. kiken, küken, D. Kieken, kuiken, G. küchkein. See Cock the animal.

chicory.etymology: F. chicorée, earlier also cichorée, L. cichorium, fr. Gr. , , Cf. Succory.

chide.etymology: imp. Chid, or Chode (Obs.); p. p. Chidden, Chid; p. pr. & vb. n. Chiding.

chief.etymology: OE. chief, chef, OF. chief, F. chef, fr. L. caput head, possibly akin to E. head. Cf. Captain, Chapter

chieftain.etymology: OE. cheftayn, chevetayn, OF. chevetain, F. capitaine, LL. capitanus, fr. L. caput head. Cf. Captain, and see chief.

chiffonier.etymology: F. chiffonnier, fem. chiffonnière, fr. chiffon rag, fr. chiffe a rag, fimsy cloth.

chignon.etymology: F., prop. equiv. to chaînon link, fr. chaîne chain, fr. L. catena Cf. Chain.

chigoe.etymology: Cf. F. chigue, perh. fr. Catalan chic small, Sp. chico; or of Peruvian origin.

child.etymology: AS. cild, pl. cildru; cf. Goth. kilÞei womb, in-kilÞ\'d3 with child.

childhood.etymology: AS. cildhad; cild child + -had. See Child, and hood.

chill.etymology: AS. cele, cyle, from the same root as celan, calan, to be cold; akin to D. kil cold, coldness, Sw. kyla to chill, and E. cool. See Cold, and cf. Cool.

roots.meaning: A New Latin plural combining form or suffix from Gr. foot; as, hexapoda, myriapoda. See -pod.

chimera.etymology: L. chimaera a chimera (in sense 1), Gr. qymbr a yearling ewe.

chimpanzee.etymology: From the native name: cf. F. chimpanzé, chimpansé, chimpanzée.

chin.etymology: AS. cin, akin to OS. kin, G kinn, Icel. kinn, cheek, Dan. & Sw. kind, L. gena, Gr. hanu. *232.

chinch.etymology: Cf. Sp. chinche, fr. L. cimex.

chink.etymology: OE. chine, AS. cine fissure, chink, fr. cinan to gape; akin to Goth. Keinan to sprout, G. keimen. Cf. Chit.

chintz.etymology: Hindi chint spotted cotton clooth, chinta spot.

chip.etymology: Cf. G. kippen to cut off the edge, to clip, pare. Cf. Chop to cut.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.
A combining form denoting divination; as, aleuromancy, chiromancy, necromancy, etc.

chirp.etymology: Of imitative orgin. Cf. Chirk, Chipper, Cheep, Chirm, Chirrup.

chisel.etymology: OF. chisel, F. ciseau, fr. LL. cisellus, prob. for caesellus, fr. L. caesus, p. p. of caedere to cut. Cf. Scissors.

chit.etymology: Cf. AS. ci shoot, sprig, from the same root as cinan to yawn. See Chink a cleft.

chitchat.etymology: From Chat, by way of reduplication.

chitterlings.etymology: Cf. AS. cwiÞ womb, Icel. kvith, Goth. qiÞus, belly, womb, stomach, G. kutteln chitterlings.

chivalrous.etymology: OF. chevalerus, chevalereus, fr. chevalier. See Chivalry.

chivalry.etymology: F. chevalerie, fr. chevalier knight, OF., horseman. See Chevalier, and cf. Cavalry.

chive.etymology: F. cive, fr. L. cepa, caepa, onion. Cf. Cives, Cibol.

roots.meaning: A suffix used to denote the salts formed from those acids whose names end in -ous; as, sulphite, from sulphurous; nitrite, from nitrous acid, etc.

chloroform.etymology: Chlorine + formyl, it having been regarded as a trichloride of this radical: cf. F. chloroforme, G. chloroform.

chock.etymology: F. choquer. Cf. Shock, v. t.

chocolate.etymology: Sp., fr. the Mexican name of the cacao. Cf. Cacao, Cocoa.

choice.etymology: OE. chois, OF. chois, F. choix, fr. choisir to choose; of German origin; cf. Goth. kausjan to examine, kiusan to choose, examine, G. kiesen. *46. Cf. Choose.

choir.etymology: OE. quer, OF. cuer, F. choeur, fr. L. chorus a choral dance, chorus, choir, fr. Gr. hortus garden, and E. yard. See Chorus.

choke.etymology: OE. cheken, choken; cf. AS. aceocian to suffocate, Icel. koka to gulp, E. chincough, cough.

choler.etymology: OE. coler, F. colère anger, L. cholera a bilious complaint, fr. Gr. Gall, and cf. Cholera.

cholera.etymology: L., a bilious disease. See Choler.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.
A suffix used in medical terms to denote a morbid condition of some part, usually some kind of tumor; as in fibroma, glaucoma.

choose.etymology: OE. chesen, cheosen, AS. ceósan; akin to OS. kiosan, D. kiezen, G. kiesen, Icel. kjosa, Goth. kiusan, L. gustare to taste, Gr. jush to enjoy. *46. Cf. Choice, 2d Gust.

chop.etymology: Cf. LG. & D. kappen, Dan. kappe, Sw. kappa. Cf. Chap to crack.

chopine.etymology: Cf. OF. chapin, escapin, Sp. chapin, Pg. chapim.

choral.etymology: LL. choralis, fr. L. chorus. See Chorus.

chord.etymology: L chorda a gut, a string made of a gut, Gr. cord. See Cord.

chore.etymology: The same word as char work done by the day.

chorus.etymology: L., a dance in a ring, a dance accompanied with song; a chorus, a band of dancers and singers. Gr. Choir.

chough.etymology: OE. choughe, kowe (and cf. OE. ca), fr. AS. ceó; cf. also D. kauw, OHG. chaha; perh. akin to E. caw. *22. Cf. Caddow.

chouse.etymology: From Turk. cha\'d4sh a messenger or interpreter, one of whom, attached to the Turkish embassy, in 1609 cheated the Turkish merchants resident in England out of £4,000.

chowder.etymology: F. chaudière a kettle, a pot. Cf. Caldron.

chrism.etymology: OE. crisme, from AS. crisma; also OE. creme, fr. OF. cresme, like the AS. word fr. LL. chrisma, fr. Gr. friare, fricare, to rub, Skr. gharsh, E. friable, friction. Cf. Chrisom.

christ.etymology: L. Christus, Gr. chri`ein to anoint. See Chrism.

christen.etymology: AS. cristnian to make a Christian, fr. cristen a Christian.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting: (a) Jurisdiction or property and jurisdiction, dominion, as in kingdom earldom. (b) State, condition, or quality of being, as in wisdom, freedom.

christian.etymology: L. christianus, Gr. cristen. See Christ.

christianity.etymology: OE. cristiente, OF. cristienté, F. chrétienté, fr. L. christianitas.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.
A suffix denoting the art of writing or describing; also, the writing or description itself; a treatise; as, calligraphy, biography, geography.

chronicle.etymology: OE. cronicle, fr. cronique, OF. cronique, F. chronique, L. chronica, fr. Gr. Chronic.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying something written, a writing; also, a writer; as autograph, crystograph, telegraph, photograph.
A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.
A combining form usually signifying an instrument for viewing (with the eye) or observing (in any way); as in microscope, telescope, altoscope, anemoscope.

chrysalis.etymology: L. chrysallis the gold- colored pupa of butterflies, Gr. Aurelia.

chrysarobin.etymology: Gr. araroba a foreign name of Goa powder + -in.

roots.meaning: A suffix. See the Note under -ine.

chthonian.etymology: Gr. in or under the earth, fr. , , earth.

chub.etymology: This word seems to signify a large or thick fish. Cf. Sw. kubb a short and thick piece of wood, and perh. F. chabot chub.

chuff.etymology: Perh. a modification of chub: cf. W. cyff stock, stump.

chum.etymology: Perh. a contraction fr. comrade or chamber fellow: cf. also AS. cuma a comer, guest.

chump.etymology: Cf. Icel. kumbr a chopping, E. chop.

church.etymology: OE. chirche, chireche, cherche, Scot. kirk, from AS. circe, cyrice; akin to D. kerk, Icel. kirkja, Sw. kyrka, Dan. kirke, G. kirche, OHG. chirihha; all fr. Gr. ç\'d4ra hero, Zend. çura strong, OIr. caur, cur, hero. Cf. Kirk.

churl.etymology: AS. ceorl a freeman of the lowest rank, man, husband; akin to D. karel, kerel, G. kerl, Dan. & Sw. karl, Icel. karl, and to the E. proper name Charles (orig., man, male), and perh. to Skr. jara lover. Cf. Carl, Charles's Wain.

churn.etymology: OE. chirne, cherne, AS. ceren, cyrin; akin to D. karn, Dan. kierne. See Churn, v. t.

chyle.etymology: NL. chylus, Gr. chyle; prob. akin to E. fuse to melt.

chyme.etymology: L. chymus chyle, Gr. chyme. See Chyle.

cicatrize.etymology: Cf. F. cicatriser, fr. cicatrice, L. cicatrix, scar.

cicerone.etymology: It., fr. L. Cicero, the Roman orator. So called from the ordinary talkativeness of such a guide.

cider.etymology: F. cidre, OF. sidre, fr. L. sicera a kind of strong drink, Gr. shakar to be intoxicated, shekar strong drink.

cigar.etymology: Sp. cigarro, orig., a kind of tobacco in the island of Cuba: cf. F. cigare.

cinch.etymology: Sp. cincha, fr. L. cingere to gird.

cinchona.etymology: So named from the wife of Count Chinchon, viceroy of Peru in the seventeenth century, who by its use was freed from an intermittent fever, and after her return to Spain, contributed to the general propagation of this remedy.

cincture.etymology: L. cinctura, fr. cingere, cinctum, to gird.

cinder.etymology: AS. sinder slag, dross; akin to Icel. sindr dross, Sw. sinder, G. sinter, D. sintel; perh. influenced by F. cendre ashes, fr. L. cinis. Cf. Sinter.

cineraria.etymology: NL., fr. LL. cinerarius pert. to ashes, fr. cinis ashes. So called from the ash-colored down on the leaves.

cinnabar.etymology: L. cinnabaris, Gr. qinbar, Hind. shangarf.

cinnamon.etymology: Heb. qinnamon; cf. Gr. cinnamomum, cinnamon. The Heb. word itself seems to have been borrowed from some other language; cf. Malay kaju manis sweet wood.

cinque.etymology: F. cinq, fr. L. quinque five. See Five.

cinquefoil.etymology: Cinque five + foil, F. feuille leaf. See Foil.

cipher.etymology: OF. cifre zero, F. Chiffre figure (cf. Sp.cifra, LL. cifra), fr. Ar. çifrun, çafrun, empty, cipher, zero, fr. çafira to be empty. Cf. Zero.

circle.etymology: OE. cercle, F. cercle, fr. L. circulus (Whence also AS. circul), dim. of circus circle, akin to Gr. Circus, Circum- .

roots.meaning: A Latin preposition, used as a prefix in many English words, and signifying around or about.

circuit.etymology: F. circuit, fr. L. circuitus, fr. circuire or circumire to go around; circum around + ire to go.

circular.etymology: L. circularis, fr. circulus circle: cf. F. circulaire. See Circle.

circulate.etymology: L. circulatus, p. p. of circulare, v. t., to surround, make round, circulari, v. i., to gather into a circle. See Circle.

circulatory.etymology: L. circulatorius pert. to a mountebank: cf. F. circulatoire.

circumambulate.etymology: L. circumambulatus, p. p. of circumambulare to walk around; circum + ambulare. See Ambulate.

circumcise.etymology: L. circumcisus, p. p. of circumcidere to cut around, to circumcise; circum + caedere to cut; akin to E. cæsura, homicide, concise, and prob. to shed, v. t.

circumflex.etymology: L. circumflexus a bending round, fr. circumflectere, circumflexum, to bend or turn about; circum + flectere to bend. See Flexible.

circumfuse.etymology: L. circumfusus, p. p. of circumfundere to pour around; circum + fundere to pour.

circumlocution.etymology: L. circumlocutio, fr. circumloqui, - locutus, to make use of circumlocution; circum + loqui to speak. See Loquacious.

circumnavigate.etymology: L. circumnavigatus, p. p. of circumnavigare to sail round; circum + navigare to navigate.

roots.meaning: A Latin preposition, used as a prefix in many English words, and signifying around or about.

circumscribe.etymology: L. circumscribere, -scriptum; circum + scribere to write, draw. See Soribe.

circumspect.etymology: L. circumspectus, p. p. of circumspicere to look about one's self, to observe; circum + spicere, specere, to look. See Spy.

circumstance.etymology: L. circumstantia, fr. circumstans, -antis, p. pr. of circumstare to stand around; circum + stare to stand. See Stand.

circumvallate.etymology: L. circumvallatus, p. p. of circumvallare to surround with a wall; circum + vallare to wall, fr. vallum rampart.

circumvent.etymology: L. circumventis, p. p. of circumvenire, to come around, encompass, decieve; circum + venire to come, akin to E. come.

circumvolve.etymology: L. circumvolvere, -volutum; circum + volvere to roll.

circus.etymology: L. circus circle, ring, circus (in sense 1). See Circle, and cf. Cirque.

cirrhosis.etymology: NL., fr. Gr. cirrhose. So called from the yellowish appearance which the diseased liver often presents when cut.

cirripedia.etymology: NL., fr. L. cirrus curl + pes, pedis, foot.

cisalpine.etymology: L. Cisalpinus; cis on this side + Alpinus Alpine.

roots.meaning: A Latin preposition, sometimes used as a prefix in English words, and signifying on this side.

cistercian.etymology: LL. Cistercium. F. Cîteaux, a convent not far from Dijon, in France: cf. F. cistercien.

cistern.etymology: OE. cisterne, OF. cisterne, F. cisterne, fr. L. cisterna, fr. cista box, chest. See Cist, and cf. chest.

citadel.etymology: F. citadelle, It. citadella, dicitt city, fr. L. civitas. See City.

citation.etymology: F. citation, LL. citatio, fr.L. citare to cite. See Cite

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

citizen.etymology: OE. citisein, OF. citeain, F. citoyen, fr. cité city. See City, and cf. Cit.

citole.etymology: OF. citole, fr. L. cithara. See Cittern.

city.etymology: OE. cite, F. citcivitas citizenship, state, city, fr. civis citizen; akin to Goth. heiwa (in heiwafrauja man of the house), AS. heirath marriage, prop., providing a house, E. hind a peasant.

civet.etymology: F. civette (cf. It. zibetto) civet, civet cat, fr. LGr. zub, zab, civet.

civic.etymology: L.civicus, fr. civis citizen. See City.

civil.etymology: L. civilis, fr. civis citizen: cf. F. civil. See City.

civility.etymology: L. civilitas: cf. F. civilité. See Civil.

civilize.etymology: Cf. F. civilizer, fr.L. civilis civil. See Civil.

clack.etymology: Prob. of imitative origin; cf. F.claquer to clap, crack, D. klakken, MHG. klac crack, Ir. clagaim I make a noise, ring. Cf. Clack, n., Clatter, Click.

claim.etymology: OE. clamen, claimen, OF. clamer, fr. L. clamare to cry out, call; akin to calare to proclaim, Gr. kal to sound, G. holen to fetch, E. hale haul.

claimant.etymology: Cf. OF. clamant, p. pr. of clamer. Cf.Clamant.

clairvoyant.etymology: F., fr. clair clear + voyant, p. pr. of voir to see. See Clear, and Vision.

clam.etymology: Cf. Clamp, Clam, v. t., Clammy.

clamant.etymology: L. clamans, p. pr. of clamare to call. Cf. Claimant.

clamatores.etymology: L. clamator, pl. clamatores, a bawler.

clamber.etymology: OE clambren, clameren, to heap together, climb; akin to Icel. klambra to clamp, G. klammern. Cf. Clamp, Climb.

clammy.etymology: Cf. AS. clam clay. See Clam to clog, and cf. Clay.

clamor.etymology: OF. clamour, clamur, F. clameur, fr. L. clamor, fr. clamare to cry out. See Claim.

clamorous.etymology: LL. clamorosus, for L. Clamosus: cf. OF. clamoreux.

clamp.etymology: Cf. LG. & D. klamp, Dan. klampe, also D. klampen to fasten, clasp. Cf. Clam, Cramp.

clan.etymology: Gael. clann offspring, descendants; akin to Ir. clann, cland, offspring, tribe, family; perh. from L. plania scion, slip, cutting. Cf. Plant, n.

clandestine.etymology: L. clandestinus, fr. clam secretly; akin to celare, E. conceal: cf. F. clandestin.

clang.etymology: L. clangere; akin to Gr. clank.

clangor.etymology: L., fr. clangere. See Clang, v. t.

clank.etymology: Akin to clink, and of imitative origin; cf. G. klang sound, D. klank. Cf. Clang.

clap.etymology: AS. clappan; akin to Icel. & Sw. klappa, D, klappen, to clap, prate, G. klaffen, v.i., to split open, yelp, klopfen, v.t. & i., to knock.

claret.etymology: OE. claret, clare, clarry, OF. claret, clar, fr. cler, F. clair, clear, fr. L. clarus clear. See Clear.

clarification.etymology: Cf. F. clarification, L. clarificatio glorification.

clarify.etymology: F. clarifier, from L. clarificare; clarus clear + facere to make. See Clear, and Fact.

clarinet.etymology: F. clarinette, dim. of clarine, from L. clarus. See Clear, and cf. Clarion.

clarion.etymology: OE. clarioun, OF. clarion, F. clairon, LL. clario, claro; so called from its clear tone, fr. L. clarus clear. See Clear.

clarity.etymology: L. claritas, fr. clarus clear: cf. F. clarté.

clash.etymology: Of imitative origin; cf. G. klatschen, Prov. G. kleschen, D. kletsen, Dan. klaske, E. clack.

clasp.etymology: OE. claspen, clapsen, prob. akin to E. clap.

class.etymology: F. classe, fr. L. classis class, collection, fleet; akin to Gr. claim, haul.

classic.etymology: L. classicus relating to the classes of the Roman people, and especially to the frist class; hence, of the first rank, superior, from classis class: cf. F. classique. See Class, n.

classical.etymology: L. classicus relating to the classes of the Roman people, and especially to the frist class; hence, of the first rank, superior, from classis class: cf. F. classique. See Class, n.

clatter.etymology: AS. cla a rattle, akin to D. klateren to rattle. Cf. Clack.

clause.etymology: F. clause, LL. clausa, equiv. to L. clausula clause, prop., close of claudere to shut, to end. See Close.

clavichord.etymology: F. clavicorde, fr. L. clavis key + chorda string.

clavicle.etymology: F. clavicule, fr. L. clavicula a little key, tendril, dim. of clavis key, akin to claudere to shut. See Close, and cf. Clef.

claw.etymology: AS. clawu, cla, cleó; akin to D. klaauw, G. Klaue, Icel. klo, SW. & Dan. klo, and perh. to E. clew.

clay.etymology: AS. clæg; akin to LG. klei, D. klei, and perh. to AS. clam clay, L. glus, gluten glue, Gr. glue. Cf. Clog.

claymore.etymology: Gael. claidheamhmor a broadsword; Gael. claidheamh sword + mor great, large. Cf. Claymore.

claytonia.etymology: Named after Dr.John Clayton, an American botanist.

clean.etymology: OE. clene, AS. cl; akin to OHG. chleini pure, neat, graceful, small, G. klein small, and perh. to W. glan clean, pure, bright; all perh. from a primitive, meaning bright, shining. Cf. Glair.

cleanse.etymology: AS. clænsian, fr. clæne clean. See Clean.

clear.etymology: OE. cler, cleer, OF. cler, F. clair, fr.L. clarus, clear, broght, loud, distinct, renownwd; perh. akin to L. clamare to call, E. claim. Cf. Chanticleer, Clairvoyant, Claret, Clarufy.

cleat.etymology: OE. clete wedge; cf.D. kloot ball, Ger. kloss, klotz, lump. clod, MHG. kloz lump, ball, wedge, OHG. chloz ball, round mass.

cleave.etymology: OE. cleovien, clivien, cliven, AS. cleofian, clifian; akin to OS. klibon, G. kleben, LG. kliven, D. kleven, Dan. klæbe, Sw. klibba, and also to G. kleiben to cleve, paste, Icel. klifa to climb. Cf. Climb.

clef.etymology: F. clef key, a key in music, fr. L. clavis key. See Clavicle.

cleft.etymology: OE. clift; cf. Sw. klyft cave, den, Icel. kluft cleft, Dan. klöft, G. kluft. See Cleave to split and cf. 2d Clift, 1st Clough.

cleg.etymology: Northern Eng. & Scot. gleg: cf. Gael. crethleag.

clemency.etymology: L. clementia, fr. clemens mild, calm.

clergy.etymology: OE. clergie, clergi, clerge, OF. clergie, F. clergie (fr. clerc clerc, fr. L. clericus priest) confused with OF. clergié, F. clergé, fr. LL. clericatus office of priest, monastic life, fr. L. clericus priest, LL. scholar, clerc. Both the Old French words meant clergy, in sense 1, the former having also sense 2. See Clerk.

cleric.etymology: AS., fr. L. clericus. See Clerk.

clerk.etymology: Either OF. clerc, fr. L. clericus a priest, or AS. clerc, cleric, clerk, priest, fr. L. clericus, fr. Gr. Clergy.

clever.etymology: Origin uncertain. Cf. OE. cliver eager, AS. clyfer (in comp.) cloven; or clifer a claw, perh. connected with E. cleave to divide, split, the meaning of E. clever perh. coming from the idea of grasping, seizing (with the mind).

clew.etymology: OE. clewe, clowe, clue, AS. cleowen, cliwen, clywe ball of thread; akin to D. kluwen, OHG. chliwa, chliuwa, G. dim. kleuel, knäuel, and perch. to L. gluma hull, husk, Skr. glaus sort of ball or tumor. Perch. akin to E. claw. *26. Cf. Knawel.

cliche.etymology: F. cliché, from clicher to stereotype.

click.etymology: Prob. an onomatopoetic word: cf. OF. cliquier. See Clack, and cf. Clink, Clique.

client.etymology: L. cliens, -emtis, for cluens, one who hears (in relation to his protector), a client, fr. L. cluere to be named or called; akin to Gr. çry, and E. loud: cf. F. client. See Loud.

cliff.etymology: AS. clif, cloef; akin to OS. klif, D. klif, klip, Icel. klif, Dan. & G. klippe, Sw. klippa; perh. orig. a climbing place. See Climb.

climate.etymology: F. climat, L. clima, -atis, fr. Gr. lean, v. i. See Lean, v. i., and cf. Clime.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

climax.etymology: L., from Gr. Ladder, Lean, v. i.

climb.etymology: AS. climban; akin to OHG. chlimban, G. & D. klimmen, Icel. klifa, and E. cleave to adhere.

clinch.etymology: OE. clenchen, prop. causative of clink to cause to clink, to strike; cf. D. klinken to tinkle, rivet. See Clink.

cling.etymology: AS. clingan to adhere, to wither; akin to Dan. klynge to cluster, crowd. Cf. Clump.

clinical.etymology: Gr. clinique. See Lean, v. i.

clink.etymology: OE. clinken; akin to G. klingen, D. klinken, SW. klinga, Dan. klinge; prob. of imitative origin. Cf. Clank, Clench, Click, v. i.

clinker.etymology: From clink; cf. D. clinker a brick which is so hard that it makes a sonorous sound, from clinken to clink. Cf. Clinkstone.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

clip.etymology: OE. cluppen, clippen, to embrace, AS. clyran to embrace, clasp; cf. OHG. kluft tongs, shears, Icel, klypa to pinch, squeeze, also OE. clippen to cut, shear, Dan. klippe to clip, cut, SW. & Icel. klippa.

clique.etymology: F., fr. OF. cliquer to click. See Click, v. i.

cloak.etymology: Of. cloque cloak (from the bell-like shape), bell, F. cloche bell; perh. of Celtik origin and the same word as E. clock. See 1st Clock.

clock.etymology: AS. clucge bell; akin to D. klok clock, bell, G. glocke, Dan. klokke, Sw. klocka, Icel. klukka bell, LL. clocca, cloca (whence F. cloche); al perh. of Celtic origin; cf. Ir. & Gael. clog bell, clock, W. cloch bell. Cf. Cloak.

clod.etymology: OE. clodde, latter form of clot. See Clot.

clog.etymology: OE. clogge clog, Scot. clag, n., a clot, v., to to obstruct, cover with mud or anything adhesive; prob. of the same origin as E. clay.

cloisonne.etymology: F., partitioned, fr. cloison a partition.

cloister.etymology: OF. cloistre, F. cloître, L. claustrum, pl. claustra, bar, bolt, bounds, fr. claudere, clausum, to close. See Close, v. t., and cf. Claustral.

close.etymology: From OF. & F. clos, p. p. of clore to close, fr. L. claudere; akin to G. schliessen to shut, and to E. clot, cloister, clavicle, conclude, sluice. Cf. Clause, n.

closet.etymology: OF. closet little inclosure, dim. of clos. See Close an inclosure.

closure.etymology: Of. closure, L. clausura, fr. clauedere to shut. See Close, v. t.

clot.etymology: OE. clot, clodde, clod; akin to D. kloot ball, G. kloss clod, dumpling, klotz block, Dan. klods, Sw. klot bowl, globe, klots block; cf. AS. clate bur. Cf. Clod, n., Clutter to clot.

cloth.etymology: OE. clath cloth, AS. cla\'ed cloth, garment; akin to D. kleed, Icel. klæ\'ebi, Dan. klæde, cloth, Sw. kläde, G. kleid garment, dress.

clothe.etymology: OE. clathen, clothen, clethen, AS. cla\'ebian, clæ\'eban. See Cloth.

cloud.etymology: Prob. fr. AS. cld a rock or hillock, the application arising from the frequent resemblance of clouds to rocks or hillocks in the sky or air.
