clout.etymology: AS. clut a little cloth, piece of metal; cf. Sw. klut, Icel. klutr a kerchief, or W. clwt a clout, Gael. clud.

clove.etymology: D. kloof. See Cleave, v. t.

clover.etymology: OE. claver, clover, AS. cl; akin to LG. & Dan. klever, D. klaver, G. klee, Sw. kl.

clown.etymology: Cf. Icel. klunni a clumsy, boorish fellow, North Fries. kl clown, dial. Sw. klunn log, Dan. klunt log block, and E. clump, n.

cloy.etymology: OE. cloer to nail up, F. clouer, fr. OF. clo nail, F. clou, fr. L. clavus nail. Cf. 3d Clove.

club.etymology: CF. Icel. klubba, klumba, club, klumbuf a clubfoot, SW. klubba club, Dan. klump lump, klub a club, G. klumpen clump, kolben club, and E. clump.

cluck.etymology: AS. cloccian; cf. D. klokken, G. glucken, glucksen, LG. klukken, Dan. klukke; all prob. of imitative origin.

clue.etymology: OE. clewe, clowe, clue, AS. cleowen, cliwen, clywe ball of thread; akin to D. kluwen, OHG. chliwa, chliuwa, G. dim. kleuel, knäuel, and perch. to L. gluma hull, husk, Skr. glaus sort of ball or tumor. Perch. akin to E. claw. *26. Cf. Knawel.

clumber.etymology: Named from the estate of the Duke of Newcastle.

clump.etymology: Cf. D. klomp lump, G. klump, klumpen, Dan. klump, Sw. kllimp; perh. akin to L. globus, E. globe. Cf. Club.

clumsy.etymology: OE. clumsed benumbed, fr. clumsen to be benumbed; cf. Icel. klumsa lockjaw, dial. Sw. klummsen benumbed with cold. Cf. 1st Clam, and 1st Clamp.

clunch.etymology: Perh. fr. clinch to make fast

cluster.etymology: AS. cluster, clyster; cf. LG. kluster (also Sw. & Dan. klase a cluster of grapes, D. klissen to be entangled.)

clutch.etymology: OE. cloche, cloke, claw, Scot. clook, cleuck, also OE. cleche claw, clechen, cleken, to seize; cf. AS. gelæccan (where ge- is a prefix) to seize. Cf. Latch a catch.

roots.meaning: An Anglo-Saxon prefix. See Y-.

clutter.etymology: Cf. W. cludair heap, pile, cludeirio to heap.

clyster.etymology: L., fr. G. hlutrs pure, G. lauter: cf. F. clystère

coach.etymology: F. coche, fr. It. cocchio, dim. of cocca little boat, fr. L. concha mussel, mussel shell, Gr. çankha. Cf. Conch, Cockboat, Cockle.

coact.etymology: L. coactare, intens. fr. cogere, coactum, to force. See Cogent.

roots.meaning: A form of the prefix com-, signifying with, together, in conjunction, joint. It is used before vowels and some consonants. See Com-.

coagulate.etymology: L. coagulatus, p. p. of coagulare to coagulate, fr. coagulum means of coagulation, fr. cogere, coactum, to drive together, coagulate. See Cogent.

coal.etymology: AS. col; akin to D. kool, OHG. chol, cholo, G. kohle, Icel. kol, pl., Sw. kol, Dan. kul; cf. Skr. jval to burn. Cf. Kiln, Collier.

coalesce.etymology: L. coalescere, coalitium; co- + alescere to grow up, incho. fr. alere to nourish. See Aliment, n.

roots.meaning: A form of the prefix com-, signifying with, together, in conjunction, joint. It is used before vowels and some consonants. See Com-.

coalition.etymology: LL. coalitio: cf. F. coalition. See Coalesce.

coarse.etymology: As this word was anciently written course, or cours, it may be an abbreviation of of course, in the common manner of proceeding, common, and hence, homely, made for common domestic use, plain, rude, rough, gross, e. g., "Though the threads be course." Gascoigne. See Course.

coast.etymology: OF. coste, F. côte, rib, hill, shore, coast, L. costa rib, side. Cf. Accost, v. t., Cutlet.

coat.etymology: OF. cote, F. cotte, petticoat, cotte d'armes coat of arms, cotte de mailles coat of mail, LL. cota, cotta, tunic, prob. of German origin; cf. OHG. chozzo coarse mantle, G. klotze, D. kot, hut, E. cot. Cf. Cot a hut.

coati.etymology: From the native name: cf. F. coati.

coax.etymology: Cf. OE. cokes fool, a person easily imposed upon, W. coeg empty, foolish; F. coquin knave, rogue.

cob.etymology: Cf. AS. cop, copp, head, top, D. kop, G. kopf, kuppe, LL. cuppa cup (cf. E. brainpan), and also W. cob tuft, spider, cop, copa, top, summit, cobio to thump. Cf. Cop top, Cup, n.

cobalt.etymology: G. kobalt, prob. fr. kobold, kobel, goblin, MHG. kobolt; perh. akin to G. koben pigsty, hut, AS. cofa room, cofgodas household gods, Icel. kofi hut. If so, the ending -old stands for older -walt, -wald, being the same as -ald in E. herald and the word would mean ruler or governor in a house, house spirit, the metal being so called by miners, because it was poisonous and troublesome. Cf. Kobold, Cove, Goblin.

cobble.etymology: From Cob a lump. See Cob, n., 9, and cf. Copple, Copplestone.

cochineal.etymology: Sp. cochinilla, dim. from L. coccineus, coccinus, scarlet, fr. coccum the kermes berry, G. Quercus coccifera; but cf. also Sp. cochinilla wood louse, dim. of cochina sow, akin to F. cochon pig.

cock.etymology: AS. coc; of unkown origin, perh. in imitation of the cry of the cock. Cf. Chicken.

cockade.etymology: F. cocarble, fr. coquard vain, OF. coquart, fr. coq cock, prob. of imitative origin. The ornament is so named from its resemblance to the crest of a cock. Cf. Coquette.

cockatrice.etymology: OF. cocatrice crocodile, F. cocatrix, cocatrice. The word is a corruption from the same source as E. crocodile, but was confused with cock the bird, F. coq, whence arose the fable that the animal was produced from a cock's egg. See Crocodile.

cocker.etymology: OE. cokeren; cf. W. cocru to indulge, fondle, E. cock the bird, F. coqueliner to dandle (Cotgrave), to imitate the crow of a cock, to run after the girls, and E. cockle, v.

cockerel.etymology: Prob. a double dim. of cock.

cockle.etymology: OE. cockes cockles, AS. s sea cockles, prob, from Celtic; cf. W. cocs cockles, Gael. cochull husk. Perh. influenced by EF. coquille shell, a dim. from the root of E. conch. Cf. Coach.

cockloft.etymology: Prop., a loft where cocks roost.

cockney.etymology: OE. cocknay, cokenay, a spoiled child, effeminate person, an egg; prob. orig. a cock's egg, a small imperfect egg; OE. cok cock + nay, neye, for ey egg (cf. Newt), AS. æg. See 1st Cock, Egg, n.

cocoon.etymology: F. cocon, dim. of coque shell of egge and insects, fr. L. concha mussel shell. See Conch.

cod.etymology: AS. codd small bag; akin to Icel. koddi pillow, Sw. kudde cushion; cf. W. cod, ciod, bag, shell.

coddle.etymology: Cf. Prov. E. caddle to coax, spoil, fondle, and Cade, a. & v. t.

codicil.etymology: L. codicillus, dim. of codex: cf. F. codicille. See Code.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.
A form of the prefix com-, signifying with, together, in conjunction, joint. It is used before vowels and some consonants. See Com-.

coerce.etymology: L. coërcere; co- + arcere to shut up, to press together. See Ark.

roots.meaning: A form of the prefix com-, signifying with, together, in conjunction, joint. It is used before vowels and some consonants. See Com-.

coercion.etymology: L. coercio, fr. coercere. See Coerce.

roots.meaning: A form of the prefix com-, signifying with, together, in conjunction, joint. It is used before vowels and some consonants. See Com-.

coeval.etymology: L. coaevus; co- + aevum lifetime, age. See Age, n.

roots.meaning: A form of the prefix com-, signifying with, together, in conjunction, joint. It is used before vowels and some consonants. See Com-.

coffee.etymology: Turk. qahveh, Ar. qahuah wine, coffee, a decoction of berries. Cf. Café.

coffer.etymology: OF. cofre, F. coffre, L. cophinus basket, fr. Gr. Coffin, n.

coffin.etymology: OE., a basket, receptacle, OF. cofin, fr. L. cophinus. See Coffer, n.

cog.etymology: Cf. W. coegio to make void, to beceive, from coeg empty, vain, foolish. Cf. Coax, v. t.

cogent.etymology: L. cogens, p. pr. of cogere to drive together, to force; co- + agere to drive. See Agent, a., and cf. Coact to force, Coagulate, p. a.

cogitable.etymology: L. cogitabilis, fr. cogitare to think.

corchorus.etymology: Nl., fr. L. corchorus a poor kind of pulse, Gr. ko`rchoros a wild plant of bitter taste.

cord.etymology: F. corde, L. chorda catgut, chord, cord, fr. Gr. haruspex soothsayer (inspector of entrails), Icel. görn, pl. garnir gut, and E. yarn. Cf. Chord, Yarn.

cordial.etymology: LL. cordialis, fr. L. cor heart: cf. F. cordial. See Heart.

cordiality.etymology: LL. cordialitas, fr. cordialis sincere: cf. F. cordialité.

cordiform.etymology: L. cor, cordis, heart + -form, cf. F. cordiforme.

cordovan.etymology: Sp. cordoban, fr. Cordova, or Cordoba, in Spain. Cf. Cordwain.

corduroy.etymology: Prob. for F. corde du roi king's cord.

coriaceous.etymology: L. coriaceous, fr. corium leather. See Cuirass.

cork.etymology: Cf. G., Dan., & Sw. kork, D. kurk; all fr. Sp. corcho, fr. L. cortex, corticis, bark, rind. Cf. Cortex.

cormorant.etymology: F. cormoran, fr. Armor. m a sea raven; m sea + bran raven, with cor, equiv. to L. corvus raven, pleonastically prefixed; or perh. fr. L. corvus marinus sea raven.

corn.etymology: L. cornu horn: cf. F. corne horn, hornlike excrescence. See Horn.

cornea.etymology: Fem. sing., fr. L. corneus horny, fr. cornu a horn. See Horn.

cornel.etymology: OF. cornille, cornoille, F. cornouille, cornel berry, LL. cornolium cornel tree, fr. L. cornus, fr. cornu horn, in allusion to the hardness of the wood. See Horn.

cornelian.etymology: F. cornaline, OF. corneline, fr. L. cornu horn. So called from its horny appearance when broken. See Horn, and cf. Carnelian.

corner.etymology: OF. corniere, cornier, LL. cornerium, corneria, fr. L. cornu horn, end, point. See Horn.

cornet.etymology: F. cornet, m. (for senses 1 & 2), cornette, f. & m. (for senses 3 & 4), dim. of corne horn, L. cornu. See Horn.

cornice.etymology: F. corniche, It. cornice, LL. coronix, cornix, fr. L. coronis a curved line, a flourish with the pen at the end of a book or chapter, Gr. corona crown. sEE Crown, and cf. Coronis.

cornucopia.etymology: L. cornu copiae horn of plenty. See Horn, and Copious.

corolla.etymology: L. corolla a little crown or garland, dim. of corona. See Crown.

corollary.etymology: L. corollarium gift, corollary, fr. corolla. See Corolla.

coronate.etymology: L. coronatus, p. p. of coronare to crown, fr. corona. See Crown.

coroner.etymology: From OE. coronen to crown, OF. coroner, fr. L. coronare, fr. corona crown. Formed as a translation of LL. coronator coroner, fr. L. corona crown, the coroner having been originally a prosecuting officer of the crown. See Crown.

coronet.etymology: Dim. of OE. corone crown; cf. OF. coronete. See Crown, and cf. Crownet, Cronet.

coronilla.etymology: NL., fr. L. corona crown: cf. F. coronille.

corozo.etymology: Cf. Sp. cerozo a kind of palm tree.

corporal.etymology: Corrupted fr. F. caporal, It. caporale, fr. capo head, chief, L. caput. See Chief, and cf. Caporal.

corporate.etymology: L. corporatus, p. p. of corporare to shape into a body, fr. corpus body. See Corpse.

corporation.etymology: L. corporatio incarnation: cf. F. corporation corporation.

corps.etymology: F., fr. L. corpus body. See Corpse.

corpse.etymology: OF. cors (sometimes written corps), F. corps, L. corpus; akin to AS. hrif womb. See Midriff, and cf. Corse, Corselet, Corps, Cuerpo.

corpulent.etymology: L. corpulentus, fr. corpus: cf. F. corpulent. See Corpse.

corrade.etymology: L. corradere, -rasum; cor- + radere to rub.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying with, together, etc. See Com-.

corral.etymology: Sp., a yard, a yard for cattle, fr. corro a circle or ring, fr. L. currere to run. Cf. Kraal.

correct.etymology: L. correctus, p. p. of corrigere to make straight, to correct; cor- + regere to lead straight: cf. F. correct. See Regular, Right, and cf. Escort.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying with, together, etc. See Com-.
A prefix signifying with, together, etc. See Com-.

correlation.etymology: LL. correlatio; L. cor- + relatio: cf. F. corrélation. Cf. Correlation.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying with, together, etc. See Com-.

correspond.etymology: Pref. cor- + respond: cf. f. correspondre.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying with, together, etc. See Com-.

corridor.etymology: F., fr. Itt. corridpore, or Sp. corredor; prop., a runner, hence, a running or long line, a gallery, fr. L. currere to run. See Course.

corrigible.etymology: LL. corribilis, fr. L. corrigere to correct: cf. F. corrigible. See Correrct.

corroborant.etymology: L. corroborans, p. pr. See Corroborate.

corroborate.etymology: L. corroboratus, p. p. of corroborare to corroborate; cor- + roborare to strengthen, robur strength. See Robust.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying with, together, etc. See Com-.

corrode.etymology: L. corrodere, -rosum; cor + rodere to gnaw: cf. F. corroder. See Rodent.

corrosion.etymology: LL. corrosio: cf. F. corrosion. See Corrode.

corrugate.etymology: L. corrugatus, p. p. of corrugare; cor-+ rugare to wrinkle, ruga wrinkle; of uncertain origin.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying with, together, etc. See Com-.

corrupt.etymology: L. corruptus, p. p. of corrumpere to corrupt; cor- + rumpere to break. See Rupture.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying with, together, etc. See Com-.

corsair.etymology: F. corsaire (cf. It. corsare, corsale, Pr. corsari), LL. corsarius, fr. L. cursus a running, course, whence Sp. corso cruise, corsa cruise, coasting voyage, corsear to cruise against the enemy, to pirate, corsario cruising, a privateer authorized to cruise against the enemy. See Course.

corse.etymology: OF. cors, F. corps. See Corpse.

corselet.etymology: F., dim. of OF. cors. F. corps, body. See Corse.

corset.etymology: F., dim. of OF. cors, F. corps, body. See Corse.

cortege.etymology: F., fr. It. corteggio train, fr. corte court. See Court.

cortical.etymology: L. cortex bark: cf. F. cortical.

coruscant.etymology: L. coruscans, p. pr. See Coruscate.

corvee.etymology: F. corvée, fr. LL. corvada, corrogata, fr. L. corrogare to entreat togetther; cor- + rogare to ask.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying with, together, etc. See Com-.

corvette.etymology: F. corvette, fr. Pg. corveta or Sp. corbeta, fr. L. corbita a slow-sailing ship of burden, fr, corbis basket. Cf. Corbeil.

cosecant.etymology: For co. secans, an abbrev. of L. complementi secans.

cosher.etymology: Ir. cosair a feast, a banquet or cf. F. coucher to lie. Cf. Couch, Coshering.

cosine.etymology: For co. sinus, an abbrev. of L. complementi sinus.

cosmetic.etymology: Gr. kosmitiko`s skilled in decorating, fr. ko`smos order, ornament: cf. F. cosmétique. See Cosmos.

cosmic.etymology: Gr. kosmiko`s of the world, fr. ko`smos: cf. F. cosmique. See Cosmos.

cosmogony.etymology: Gr. kosmogoni`a; ko`smos the world + root of gi`gnesthai to be born: cf. F. cosmogonie.

cosmology.etymology: Gr. ko`smos the world + -logy: cf. F. cosmologie.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

cosmos.etymology: NL., fr. Gr. ko`smos order, harmony, the world (from its perfect order and arrangement); akin to Skr. to distinguish one's self.

coss.etymology: Cf. Pers. k a road measure of about two miles; or Skr. kr.

cossack.etymology: Russ. kozak', kazak': cf. Turk. kaz.

cosset.etymology: Cf. AS. cotsetla cottager, G. kossat, kothsasse, fr. kot, koth E. (cot) hut, and cf. also E. cade, a., cot a cade lamb.

costive.etymology: OF. costev, p. p. of costever, F. constiper, L. constipare to press closely together, to cram; con- + stipare to press together, cram. See Stipulate, Stiff, and cf. Constipate.

roots.meaning: - (cum, signifying with, together, etc. See Com-.

costmary.etymology: L. costum an Oriental aromatic plant (Gr. kost, kust) + Maria Mary. Cf.Alecost.

costume.etymology: F. costume, It. costume custom, dress, fr. L. consuetumen (not found), for consuetudo custom. See Custom, and cf. Consuetude.

cot.etymology: OE. cot, cote, AS. cot, cote, cottage; akin to D. & Icel. kot, G. koth, kot, kothe. Cf. Coat.

cotangent.etymology: For co. tangens, an abbrev. of L. complementi tangens. See Tangent.

coterie.etymology: F., prob. from OF. coterie servile tenure, fr. colier cotter; of German origin. See 1st Cot.

cotillion.etymology: F. cotillon, fr. OF. cote coat, LL. cotta tunic. See Coat.

cotswold.etymology: Cot a cottage or hut + wold an open country.

cottar.etymology: LL. cotarius, cottarius, coterius. See Cot.

cotter.etymology: LL. cotarius, cottarius, coterius. See Cot.

cottier.etymology: OF. cotier. See Coterie, and cf. Cotter.

cotton.etymology: F. coton, Sp. algodon the cotton plant and its wool, coton printed cotton, cloth, fr. Ar. qutun, alqutun, cotton wool. Cf. Acton, Hacqueton.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

couch.etymology: F. coucher to lay down, lie down, OF. colchier, fr. L. collocare to lay, put, place; col- + locare to place, fr. locus place. See Locus.

roots.meaning: - (with, together. See Com-.

couchant.etymology: F., p. pr. of coucher. See Couch, v. t.

cougar.etymology: F. couguar, from the native name in the South American dialects, cuguacuara, cuguacuarana.

cough.etymology: Cf. D. kuchen, MHG. k to breathe, G. keuchen to pant, and E. chincough, the first part of which is prob. akin to cough; cf. also E. choke.

coulisse.etymology: F., fr. couler to flow, glide.

coulomb.etymology: From Coulomb, a French physicist and electrican.

council.etymology: F. concile, fr. L. concilium; con- + calare to call, akin to Gr. hale, v., haul. Cf. Conciliate. This word is often confounded with counsel, with which it has no connection.

roots.meaning: - (cum, signifying with, together, etc. See Com-.

counsel.etymology: OE. conc, F. conseil, fr. L. consilium, fr. the root of consulere to consult, of uncertain origin. Cf. Consult, Consul.

counselor.etymology: OE. conseiler, F. conseiller, fr. L. consiliarius, fr. consilium counsel.

count.etymology: OF. conter, and later (etymological spelling) compter, in modern French thus distinguished; conter to relate (cf. Recount, Account), compter to count; fr. L. computuare to reckon, compute; com- + putare to reckon, settle, order, prune, orig., to clean. See Pure, and cf. Compute.

roots.meaning: A prefix from the Latin preposition cum, signifying with, together, in conjunction, very, etc. It is used in the form com- before b, m, p, and sometimes f, and by assimilation becomes col- before l, cor- before r, and con- before any consonant except b, h, l, m, p, r, and w. Before a vowel com- becomes co-; also before h, w, and sometimes before other consonants.

countenance.etymology: OE. contenance, countenaunce, demeanor, composure, F. contenance demeanor, fr. L. continentia continence, LL. also, demeanor, fr. L. continere to hold together, repress, contain. See Contain, and cf. Continence.

counter.etymology: OE. countere, countour, a counter (in sense 1), OF. contere, conteor, fr. conter to count. See Count, v. t.

counterfeit.etymology: F. contrefait, p. p. of contrefaire to counterfeit; contre (L. contra) + faire to make, fr. L. facere. See Counter, adv., and Fact.

countermand.etymology: F. contremander; contre (L. contra) + mander to command, fr. L. mandare. Cf. Mandate.

countermine.etymology: Counter- + mine underground gallery: cf. F. contermine.

counterpane.etymology: See Counterpoint, corrupted into counterpane, from the employment of pane-shaped figures in these coverlets.

counterpoise.etymology: OE. countrepesen, counterpeisen, F. contrepeser. See Counter, adv., and Poise, v. t.

countervail.etymology: OF. contrevaloir; contre (L. contra) + valoir to avail, fr. L. valere to be strong, avail. See Vallant.

countess.etymology: F. comtesse. See Count a nobleman.

country.etymology: F. contr, LL. contrata, fr. L. contra over against, on the opposite side. Cf. Counter, adv., Contra.

county.etymology: F. comt, fr. LL. comitatus. See Count.

coupe.etymology: F., fr. coupé, p. p. of couper to cut. See Coppice.

couple.etymology: F. couple, fr. L. copula a bond, band; co- + apere, aptum, ti join. See Art, a., and cf.Copula.

roots.meaning: A form of the prefix com-, signifying with, together, in conjunction, joint. It is used before vowels and some consonants. See Com-.

couplet.etymology: F. couplet, dim. of couple. See Couple, n.

coupon.etymology: F., fr. couper to cut, cut off. See Coppice.

courage.etymology: OE. corage heart, mind, will, courage, OF. corage, F. courage, fr. a LL. derivative of L. cor heart. See Heart.

courbaril.etymology: F. courbaril, from a South American word.

courier.etymology: F. courrier, fr. courre, courir, to run, L. currere. See Course, Current.

course.etymology: F. cours, course, L. cursus, fr. currere to run. See Current.

court.etymology: OF. court, curt, cort, F. co, LL. cortis, fr. L. cohors, cors, chors, gen. cohortis, cortis, chortis, an inclosure, court, thing inclosed, crowd, throng; co- + a root akin to Gr. garden, yard, orchard. See Yard, and cf. Cohort, Curtain.

roots.meaning: A form of the prefix com-, signifying with, together, in conjunction, joint. It is used before vowels and some consonants. See Com-.

courteous.etymology: OE. cortais, corteis, cortois, rarely corteous, OF. corties, corteis, F. courtois. See Court.

courtesan.etymology: F. courtisane, fr. courtisan courtier, It. cortigiano; or directly fr. It. cortigiana, or Sp. cortesana. See Court.

courtesy.etymology: OE. cortaisie, corteisie, courtesie, OF. curteisie, cortoisie, OF. curteisie, cortoisie, F. courtoisie, fr. curteis, corteis. See Courteous.

cousin.etymology: F. cousin, LL. cosinus, cusinus, contr. from L. consobrinus the child of a mother's sister, cousin; con- + sobrinus a cousin by the mother's side, a form derived fr. soror (forsosor) sister. See Sister, and cf. Cozen, Coz.

roots.meaning: - (cum, signifying with, together, etc. See Com-.

cove.etymology: AS. cofa room; akin to G. koben pigsty, orig., hut, Icel kofi hut, and perh. to E. cobalt.

covenant.etymology: OF. covenant, fr. F. & OF. convenir to agree, L. convenire. See Convene.

cover.etymology: OF. covrir, F. couvrir, fr. L. cooperire; co- + operire to cover; probably fr. ob towards, over + the root appearing in aperire to open. Cf. Aperient, Overt, Curfew.

roots.meaning: A form of the prefix com-, signifying with, together, in conjunction, joint. It is used before vowels and some consonants. See Com-.

coverlet.etymology: F. couvre-lit; couvrir to cover + lit bed, fr. L. lectus bed. See Cover.

covert.etymology: OF. covert, F. couvert, p. p. of couvrir. See Cover, v. t.

covet.etymology: OF. coveitier, covoitier, F. convoiter, from a derivative fr. L. cupere to desire; cf. Skr. kup to become excited. Cf. Cupidity.

covetous.etymology: OF. coveitos, F. convoiteux. See Covet, v. t.

covey.etymology: OF. cov, F. couv, fr. cover, F. couver, to sit or brood on, fr. L. cubare to lie down; cf. E. incubate. See Cubit, and cf. Cove to brood.

coward.etymology: OF. couard, coard, coart, n. and adj., F. couard, fr. OF. coe, coue, tail, F. queue (fr. L. coda, a form of cauda tail) + -ard; orig., short-tailed, as an epithet of the hare, or perh., turning tail, like a scared dog. Cf. Cue, Queue, Caudal.

roots.meaning: The termination of many English words; as, coward, reynard, drunkard, mostly from the French, in which language this ending is of German origin, being orig. the same word as English hard. It usually has the sense of one who has to a high or excessive degree the quality expressed by the root; as, braggart, sluggard.

cowardice.etymology: F. couardise, fr. couard. See Coward.

cower.etymology: Cf. Icel. kera to doze, liequiet, Sw. kura, Dan. kure, G. kauern to cower, W. cwrian.

cowherd.etymology: AS. c; c cow + hyrde a herder.

cowl.etymology: AS cuhle, cugle, cugele; cf. dial. G. kogel, gugel, OF. coule, goule; all fr. LL. cuculla, cucullus, fr. L. cucullus cap, hood; perh. akin to celare to conceal, cella cell. Cf. Cucullate.

cowslip.etymology: AS. c, c, prob. orig., cow's droppings. Cf. Slop, n.

coxcomb.etymology: A corrupted spelling of cock's comb.

coy.etymology: OE. coi quiet, still, OF. coi, coit, fr.L. quietus quiet, p. p. of quiescere to rest, quie rest; prob. akin to E. while. See While, and cf. Quiet, Quit, Quite.

cozen.etymology: From cousin, hence, literally, to deceive through pretext of relationship, F. cousiner.

cozy.etymology: Cf. Scot. cosie, cozie, prob. from Gael. cosach abounding in hollows, or cosagach full of holes or crevices, snug, sheltered, from cos a hollow, a crevice.

crab.etymology: AS. crabba; akin to D. krab, G. krabbe, krebs, Icel. krabbi, Sw. krabba, Dan. krabbe, and perh. to E. cramp. Cf. Crawfish.

crack.etymology: OE. cracken, craken, to crack, break, boast, AS. cracian, cearcian, to crack; akin to D. kraken, G. krachen; cf. Skr. garj to rattle, or perh. of imitative origin. Cf. Crake, Cracknel, Creak.

cradle.etymology: AS. cradel, cradol, prob. from Celtic; cf. Gael. creathall, Ir. craidhal, W. cryd a shaking or rocking, a cradle; perh. akin to E. crate.

craft.etymology: AS. cr strength, skill, art, cunning; akin to OS., G., Sw., & Dan. kraft strength, D. kracht, Icel. kraptr; perh. originally, a drawing together, stretching, from the root of E. cramp.

crag.etymology: W. craig; akin to Gael. creag, Corn. karak, Armor. karrek.

cram.etymology: AS. crammian to cram; akin to Icel. kremia to squeeze, bruise, Sw. krama to press. Cf. Cramp.

cramp.etymology: OE. crampe, craumpe; akin to D. & Sw. kramp, Dan. krampe, G. krampf (whence F. crampe), Icel. krappr strait, narrow, and to E. crimp, crumple; cf. cram. See Grape.

cranberry.etymology: So named from its fruit being ripe in the spring when the cranes return. Dr. Prior.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.
A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

crank.etymology: OE. cranke; akin to E. cringe, cringle, crinkle, and to crank, a., the root meaning, probably, "to turn, twist." See Cringe.

cranny.etymology: F. cran notch, prob. from L. crena (a doubful word).

crape.etymology: F. cr, fr. L. crispus curled, crisped. See Crisp.

crapulent.etymology: L. crapulentus, crapulosus: cf. F. crapuleux.

crapulous.etymology: L. crapulentus, crapulosus: cf. F. crapuleux.

crash.etymology: OE. crashen, the same word as crasen to break, E. craze. See Craze.

crass.etymology: L. crassus thick, fat, gross, prob. orig., closely woven See Crease animal fat, and cf. Crate, Hurdle.

crate.etymology: L. cratis hurdle; perh. akin to E. cradle. See Hurdle, and cf. Crate a framework.

crater.etymology: L. crater, cratera, a mixing vessel, the mouth of a volcano, Gr. ir to cook, Crail, in Holy Grail.

cravat.etymology: F. cravate, fr. Cravate a Croat, an inhabitant of Croatia, one of a body of Austrian troops, from whom, in 1636, this article of dress was adopted in France.

crave.etymology: AS. crafian; akin to Icel. krefia, Sw. kr, Dan. kr.

craven.etymology: OE. cravant, cravaunde, OF. cravant struck down, p. p. of cravanter, crevanter, to break, crush, strike down, fr. an assumed LL. crepantare, fr. L. crepans, p. pr. of crepare to break, crack, rattle. Cf. Crevice, Crepitate.

craw.etymology: Akin to D. kraag neck, collar, G. kragen, Sw. kr craw, Dan. kro, and possibly to Gr.bronchus), or Crag neck.

crawfish.etymology: Corrupted fr. OE. crevis, creves, OF. crevice, F. , fr. OHG. krebiz crab, G. krebs. See Crab. The ending -fish arose from confusion with E. fish.

crawl.etymology: Dan. kravle, or Icel. krafla, to paw, scrabble with the hands; akin to Sw. kr to crawl; cf. LG. krabbeln, D. krabbelen to scratch.

crayfish.etymology: Corrupted fr. OE. crevis, creves, OF. crevice, F. , fr. OHG. krebiz crab, G. krebs. See Crab. The ending -fish arose from confusion with E. fish.

crayon.etymology: F., a crayon, a lead pencil (crayon Conté Conté's pencil, i. e., one made a black compound invented by Conté), fr. craie chalk, L. creta; said to be, properly, Cretan earth, fr. Creta the island Crete. Cf. Cretaceous.

craze.etymology: OE. crasen to break, fr. Scand., perh. through OF.; cf. Sw. krasa to crackle, sl, to break to pieces, F. to crush, fr. the Scand. Cf. Crash.

creak.etymology: OE. creken, prob. of imitative origin; cf. E. crack, and. D. kreiken to crackle, chirp.

cream.etymology: F. cr, perh. fr. LL. crema cteam of milk; cf. L. cremor thick juice or broth, perh. akin to cremare to burn.

crease.etymology: Cf. LG. krus, G. krause, crispness, krausen, kr, to crisp, curl, lay on folds; or perh. of Celtic origin; cf. Armor.kriz a wrinkle, crease, kriza to wrinkle, fold, W. crych a wrinkle, crychu to rumple, ripple, crease.

create.etymology: L. creatus, p. p. of creare to create; akin to Gr. k to make, and to E. ending -cracy in aristocracy, also to crescent, cereal.

creation.etymology: L. creatio: cf. F. cr. See Create.

creature.etymology: F. cr, L. creatura. See Create.

credence.etymology: LL. credentia, fr. L. credens, -entis, p. pr. of credere to trust, believe: cf. OF. credence. See Creed, and cf. Credent, Creance.

credential.etymology: Cf. It. credenziale, fr. LL. credentia. See Credence.

credible.etymology: L. credibilis, fr. credere. See Creed.

credit.etymology: F. cr (cf. It. credito), L. creditum loan, prop. neut. of creditus, p. p. of credere to trust, loan, believe. See Creed.

creditor.etymology: L.: cf. F. cr. See Credit.

credulity.etymology: L. credulitas, fr. credulus: cf. F. cr. See Credulous.

credulous.etymology: L. credulus, fr. credere. See Creed.

creed.etymology: OE. credo, crede, AS. creda, fr. L. credo I believe, at the beginning of the Apostles' creed, fr. credere to believe; akin to OIr. cretin I believe, and Skr. ; crat trust + dh to put. See Do, v. t., and cf. Credo, Grant.

creek.etymology: AS. crecca; akin to D. kreek, Icel. kriki crack, nook; cf. W. crig crack, crigyll ravine, creek. Cf. Crick, Crook.

creep.etymology: OE. crepen, creopen, AS. cre; akin to D. kruipen, G. kriechen, Icel. krjupa, Sw. krypa, Dan. krybe. Cf. Cripple, Crouch.

cremate.etymology: L. crematus, p. p. of cremare to burn; cf. Skr. cr to cook.

crenel.etymology: OF. crenel, F. cr, LL. crenellus, kernellus, dim. (prob.) fr. L. crena notch. See Crenny.

crenelate.etymology: LL. crenellare, kernellare: cf. F. cr to indent. See Crenelle.

crenelle.etymology: OF. crenel, F. cr, LL. crenellus, kernellus, dim. (prob.) fr. L. crena notch. See Crenny.

creole.etymology: F. cr, Sp. criollo, from an American negro word, perh. a corruption of a Sp. criadillo, dim. of criado servant, formerly also, child, fr. L. creatus, p. p. of creare to create. Cf. Create.

crepitate.etymology: L. crepitatus, p. p. of crepitare to crackle, v. intensive of crepare to crack. Cf. Crevice.

crepuscle.etymology: L. crepusculum, fr. creper dusky, dark: cf. F. cr.

crepuscule.etymology: L. crepusculum, fr. creper dusky, dark: cf. F. cr.

crescendo.etymology: It., from crescere to increase. See Crescent.

crescent.etymology: OE. cressent, cressaunt, crescent (in sense 1), OF. creissant increasing, F. croissant, p. pr. of cro, OF. creistre, fr. L. crescere to increase, v. incho.; akin to creare to create. See Create, and cf. Accrue, Increase, Crescendo.

cress.etymology: OE. ces, cresse, kers, kerse, AS. cresse, cerse; akin to D. kers, G. kresse, Dan. karse, Sw. krasse, and possibly also to OHG. chresan to creep.

crest.etymology: OF. creste, F. cr, L. crista.

cretaceous.etymology: L. cretaceus, fr. creta chalk. See Crayon.

cretonne.etymology: F., gr. Creton, its first manufacturer.

crevice.etymology: OE. crevace, crevice. F. crevasse, fr. crever to break, burst, fr. L. crepare to crack,break. Cf. Craven, Crepitate, Crevasse.

crew.etymology: From older accrue accession, reAccrue, Crescent.

crib.etymology: AS. crybb; akin to OS. kribbja, D. krib, kribbe, Dan. krybbe, G. krippe, and perh. to MHG. krebe basket, G, korb, and E. rip a sort of wicker basket.

cricket.etymology: OE. criket, OF. crequet, criquet; prob. of German origin, and akin to E. creak; cf. D. kriek a cricket. See Creak.

crime.etymology: F. crime, fr. L. crimen judicial decision, that which is subjected to such a decision, charge, fault, crime, fr. the root of cernere to decide judicially. See Certain.

criminal.etymology: L. criminalis, fr. crimen: cf. F. criminel. See Crime.

criminality.etymology: LL. criminalitas, fr. L. criminalis. See Criminal.

criminate.etymology: L. criminatus, p. p. of criminare, criminari, to criminate, fr. crimen. See Crime.

crimp.etymology: Akin to D. krimpen to shrink, shrivel, Sw. krympa, Dan. krympe, and to E. cramp. See Cramp.

crimson.etymology: OE. crimson, OF. crimoisin, F. cramoisi (cf. Sp. carmesi.) LL. carmesinus, fr. Ar. qermazi, fr. qermez crimson, kermes, fr. Skr. k produced by a worm; k worm or insect + jan to generate; akin to E. kin. CF. Carmine, Kermes.

cringe.etymology: As. crincgang, cringan, crincan, to jield, fall; akin to E. crank.

cringle.etymology: Icel. kringla orb; akin to kring around, and to D. kring circle, and to E. cringe, crank.

crinkle.etymology: A dim., fr. the root of cringe; akin to D. krinkelen to wind or twist. Cf. Cringle, Cringe.

crinoidea.etymology: NL., from Gr. -oid: cf. F. crino.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

cripple.etymology: OE. cripel, crepel, crupel, AS. crypel (akin to D. kreuple, G. kr, Dan. kr, Icel. kryppill), prop., one that can not walk, but must creep, fr. AS. cre to creep. See Creep.

crisp.etymology: AS. crisp, fr. L. crispus; cf. carpere to pluck, card (wool), and E. harvest. Cf. Crape.

crispate.etymology: L. crispatus, p. p. of crispare.

critic.etymology: L. criticus, Gr. able to discuss, from Certain, and cf. Critique.

criticise.etymology: Written also, more analogically, but less commonly, criticize.

critique.etymology: F. critique, f., fr. Gr. Critic.

croak.etymology: From the primitive of AS. cracettan to croak as a raven; akin to G. kr to croak, and to E. creak, crake.

crochet.etymology: F. crochet small hook. See Croche.

crock.etymology: Cf. W. croeg cover, Scot. crochit covered.

crocket.etymology: OF. croquet, F. crochet, dim. of croc hook. See Crook, and cf. Crotchet.

crocodile.etymology: L. crocodilus, Gr. crocodile. Cf. Cookatrice.

crocus.etymology: L., saffron, fr. Gr. kark, Ar. kurkum, Skr. ku.

croft.etymology: AS. croft; akin to D. kroft hillock; cf. Gael. croit hump, croft.

cromlech.etymology: W. cromlech; crom bending or bent, concave + llech a flat stone; akin to Ir. cromleac.

crone.etymology: OD. kronie, karonie, an old sheep, OF. carogne, F. charogne, carrion (also F. carogne illnatured woman.). See Carrion, and Crony.

crony.etymology: Orig., an old woman. See Crone.

crook.etymology: OE. crok; akin to Icel. kr hook,bend, SW. krok, Dan. krog, OD. krooke; or cf. Gael. crecan crook, hook, W. crwca crooked. Cf. Crosier, Crotchet, Crutch, Encroach.

crop.etymology: OE. crop, croppe, craw, top of a plant, harvest, AS. crop, cropp, craw, top, bunch, ear of corn; akin to D. krop craw, G. kropf, Icel. kroppr hump or bunch on the body, body; but cf. also W. cropa, croppa, crop or craw of a bird, Ir. & Gael. sgroban. Cf. Croup, Crupper, Croup.

croquet.etymology: From French; cf. Walloon croque blow, fillip. F. croquet a crisp biscuit, croquer to crunch, fr. croc a crackling sound, of imitative origin. Croquet then properly meant a smart tap on the ball.

crosier.etymology: OE. rocer, croser, croyser, fr. croce crosier, OF. croce, croche, F. crosse, fr. LL. crocea, crocia, from the same German or Celtic sourse as F. croc hook; akin to E. crook.

cross.etymology: OE. crois, croys, cros; the former fr. OF. crois, croiz, F. croix, fr. L. crux; the second is perh. directly fr. Prov. cros, crotz. fr. the same L. crux; cf. Icel. kross. Cf. Crucial, Crusade, Cruise, Crux.

crotchet.etymology: F. crochet, prop., a little hook, a dim. from the same source as croc hook. See Crook, and cf. Crochet, Crocket, Crosier.

crouch.etymology: OE. cruchen, crouchen, crouken; cf. E. creep, G. krauchen, kriechen, or E. crook to bend, also crouch to cross.

croup.etymology: F. croupe hind quarters, croup, rump, of German or Icel. origin; cf. Icel. kryppa hump; akin to Icel. kroppr. Cf. Crop.

croupier.etymology: F.; prop., one who sits on the croup, and hence, in the second place; an assistant. See 1st Croup.

crouton.etymology: F. cro, fr. cro a crust.

crow.etymology: AS. cr; akin to D. kraijen, G. kr, cf. Lith. groti to croak. sq. root24. Cf. Crake.

crowd.etymology: OE. crouden, cruden, AS. cr; cf. D. kruijen to push in a wheelbarrow.

crown.etymology: OE. corone, coroun, crune, croun, OF. corone, corune, F. couronne, fr. L. corona crown, wreath; akin to Gr. curvus curved, E. curve, curb, Gael. cruinn round, W. crwn. Cf. Cornice, Corona, Coroner, Coronet.

crucial.etymology: F. crucial, fr. L. crux, crucis, cross, torture. See Cross.

cruciate.etymology: L. cruciatus, p. p. of cruciare to crucify, torture, fr. crux, crucis, a cross. See Cross.

crucible.etymology: LL. crucubulum a hanging lamp, an earthen pot for melting metals (cf. OF. croisel, creuseul, sort of lamp, crucible, F. creuset crucible), prob. of German origin; cf. OHG. kr, LG. kr, hanging lamp, kroos, kruus, mug, jug, jar, D. kroes cup, crucible, Dan. kruus, Sw. krus, E. cruse. It was confused with derivatives of L. crux cross (cf. Crosslet), and crucibles were said to have been marked with a cross, to prevent the devil from marring the chemical operation. See Cruse, and cf. Cresset.

cruciferous.etymology: L. crux, crucis, cross + - ferous: cf. F. crucif.

crucifix.etymology: F. crucifix or LL. crucifixum, fr. L. crux, crucis, cross + figere, fixum, to fix. See Cross, and Fix, and cf. Crucify.

cruciform.etymology: L. crux, crucis, cress + -form: cf. F. cruciforme.

crucify.etymology: F. crucifier, fr. (assumed) LL. crucificare, for crucifigere, fr, L. crux, crucis, cross + figere to fix, the ending - figere being changed to -ficare, F. -fier (in compounds), as if fr. L. facere to do, make. See Cross, and Fix, and cf. Crucifix.

crude.etymology: L. crudus raw; akin to cruor blood (which flows from a wound). See Raw, and cf. Cruel.

crudity.etymology: L. cruditas, fr. crudus: cf. F. crudit. See Crude.

cruel.etymology: F. cruel, fr. L. crudelis, fr. crudus. See Crude.

cruelty.etymology: OF. cruelt, F. cruaut, fr. L. crudelitas, fr. crudelis. See Cruel.

cruet.etymology: Anglo-French cruet, a dim. from OF. crue, cruie; of German or Celtic origin, and akin to E. crock an earthen vessel.

cruise.etymology: D. kruisen to move crosswise or in a zigzag, to cruise, fr. kruis cross, fr. OF. crois, croiz, F. croix, or directly fr. OF. croisier, F. croiser, to cross, cruise, fr. crois a cross. See Cross.

crumb.etymology: AS. cruma, akin to D. kruim, G. krume; cf. G. krauen to scratch, claw.

crumble.etymology: Dim. of crumb, v. t., akin to D. krimelen G. kr.

crump.etymology: AS. crumb stooping, bent down; akin to OHG. chrumb, G. krumm, Dan. krum, D. krom, and E. cramp.

crumpet.etymology: Prob. from W. crempog, crammwgth, a pancake or fritter.

crunch.etymology: Prob. of imitative origin; or cf. D. schransen to eat heartily, or E. scrunch.

crupper.etymology: F. croupi, fr. croupe. See Croup the rump of a horse.

crural.etymology: L. cruralis, fr. crus, cruris, leg: cf. F. crural.

crusade.etymology: F. croisade, fr. Pr. crozada, or Sp cruzada, or It. crociata, from a verb signifying to take the cross, mark one's self with a cross, fr. L. crux cross; or possibly taken into English directly fr. Pr. Cf. Croisade, Crosado, and see Cross.

cruse.etymology: Akin to LG. kruus, kroos, mug, jug, jar, D. kroes, G. krause, Icel. krus, Sw. krus, Dan. kruus. Cf. Crucible, Cresset.

crush.etymology: OE. cruschen, crousshen, Of. cruisir, croissir, fr. LL. cruscire, prob. of Ger. origin, from a derivative of the word seen in Goth. kruistan to gnash; akin to Sw. krysta to squeeze, Dan. kryste, Icel. kreysta.

crust.etymology: L. crusta: cf. OF. crouste, F. cro; prob. akin to Gr. crystal, from the same root as E. crude, raw. See Raw, and cf. Custard.

crustacea.etymology: Neut. pl. of NL. crustaceus pert. to the crust or shell, from L. crusta the hard surfsce of a body, rind, shell.

crutch.etymology: OE. cruche, AS. crycc, cricc; akin to D. kruk, G. kr, Dan. krykke, Sw. krycka, and to E. crook. See Crook, and cf. Cricket a low stool.

cry.etymology: F. crier, cf. L. quiritare to raise a plaintive cry, scream, shriek, perh. fr. queri to complain; cf. Skr. cvas to pant, hiss, sigh. Cf. Quarrel a brawl, Querulous.

roots.meaning: Combining forms fr. Gr. li`qos a stone; -- used chiefly in naming minerals and rocks.
A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

crypt.etymology: L. crypta vault, crypt, Gr. Crot, Crotto.

cryptogamia.etymology: NL., fr. Gr. krypto`s hidden, secret + ga`mos marriage.

cryptograph.etymology: Gr. krypto`s hidden + -graph: cf. F. cryptographe.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying something written, a writing; also, a writer; as autograph, crystograph, telegraph, photograph.
A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

crystal.etymology: OE. cristal, F. cristal, L. crystallum crystal, ice, fr. Gr. crystalla, fr. L. crystallum; prob. akin to E. crust. See Crust, Raw.

crystalline.etymology: L. crystallinus, from Gr. cristallin. See Crystal.

crystallography.etymology: Gr. -graphy: cf. F. cristallographie. See Crystal.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting the art of writing or describing; also, the writing or description itself; a treatise; as, calligraphy, biography, geography.

cub.etymology: Cf. Ir. cuib cub, whelp, young dog, Ir. & Gael. cu dog; akin to E. hound.

cubeb.etymology: F. cub (cf. It. cubebe, Pr., Sp., Pg., & NL. cubeba), fr. Ar. kab.

cubic.etymology: L. cubicus, Gr. cubique. See Cube.

cubical.etymology: L. cubicus, Gr. cubique. See Cube.

cubit.etymology: L. cubitum, cubitus; elbow, ell, cubit, fr. (because the elbow serves focubare to lie down, recline; cf. Gr. Incumbent, Covey.

cuckold.etymology: OE. kukeweld, cokewold, cokold, fr. OF. coucoul, cucuault, the last syllable being modified by the OE. suffix -wold (see Herald); cf. F. cocu a cuckold, formerly also, a cuckoo, and L. cuculus a cuckoo. The word alludes to the habit of the female cuckoo, who lays her eggs in the nests of other birds, to be hatched by them.

cuckoo.etymology: OE. coccou, cukkow, F. coucou, prob. of imitative origin; cf. L. cuculus, Gr. k, G. kuckuk, D. koekoek.

cucumber.etymology: OE. cucumer, cocumber, cucumber, fr. L. cucmis, gen.cucumeris; cf. OF. cocombre,F. concombre.

cucurbit.etymology: L. cucurbita a gourd: cf. F. cucurbite. See Gourd.

cud.etymology: AS. cudu, cwudu,cwidu,cweodo, of uncertain origin; cf, G. k bait, Icel. kvi womb, Goth. qipus. Cf. Quid.

cudbear.etymology: Also cudbeard, corrupted fr. the name of Dr. Cuthbert Gordon, a Scotchman, who first brought it into notice.

cuddle.etymology: Prob. for couthle, fr. couth known; cf. OE. kuppen to cuddle, or cu to make friends with. SeeCouth, Uncouth, Can.

cudgel.etymology: OE. kuggel; cf. G. keule club (with a round end), kugel ball, or perh. W. cogyl cudgel, or D. cudse, kuds, cudgel.

cudweed.etymology: Apparently fr. cud. + weed, but perh. a corruption of cottonweed; or of cut weed, so called from its use as an application to cuts and chafings.

cue.etymology: OF. coue, coe, F. queue, fr. L. coda, cauda, tail. Cf. Caudal, Coward, Queue.

cuff.etymology: Cf. Sw. kuffa to knock, push,kufva to check, subdue, and E. cow, v. t.

cuirass.etymology: F.cuirasse, orig., a breascuir, cuirie influenced by It. corazza, or Sp. cora, fr. an assumed LL. coriacea, fr. L. coriacevs, adj., of leather, fr. corium leather, hide; akin to Gr. skora hide, Lith. skura hide, leather. Cf. Coriaceous.

cuisine.etymology: F., fr. L. coquina kitchen, fr. coquere to cook. See Kitchen.

culinary.etymology: L. culinarius, fr. culina kitchen, perh. akin to carbo coal: cf. F. culinare.

cull.etymology: OE., OF. cuillir, coillir, F.cueillir, to gather, pluck, pick, fr. L. colligere. See Coil, v. t., and cf. Collect.

cullis.etymology: OF. coleïs, F. coulis, fr. OF. & F. couler to strain, to flow, fr. L. colare to filter, strain; cf. LL. coladicium. Cf. Colander.

culm.etymology: L. culmus stark, stem; akin to colasmus. SeeHalm.

culminate.etymology: L. cuimen top or ridge. See Column.

culpable.etymology: OE. culpable, coulpable, coupable, F. coupable, formerly also coupable, formerly also coulpable, culpable, fr. L. culpabilis, fr. culpare to blame, fr. culpa fault.

culprit.etymology: Prob. corrupted for culpate, fr. Law Latin culpatus the accused, p. p. of L. culpare to blame. See Culpable.

cult.etymology: F. culte, L. cultus care, culture, fr. colere to cultivate. Cf. Cultus.

cultivate.etymology: LL. cultivatus, p.p. of cultivare to cultivate, fr. cultivus cultivated, fr. L. cultus, p.p. of colere to till, cultivate. Cf. Colony.

culture.etymology: F. culture, L. cultura, fr. colere to till, cultivate; of uncertain origin. Cf. Colony.

culverin.etymology: F. coulevrine, prop. fem. of couleuvrin like a serpent, fr. couleuvre adder, fr. L. coluber, colubra.

culvert.etymology: Prob. from OF. coulouere, F. couloir, channel, gutter, gallery, fr. couler to flow. See Cullis.

cumber.etymology: OE. combren, cumbren,OF. combrer to hinder, from LL. cumbrus a heap, fr. L. cumulus; cf. Skr. to increase, grow strong. Cf. Cumulate.

cumin.etymology: OE.comin, AS. cymen, fr. L. cuminum, Gr.kamm, Heb. kamm; cf. OF. comin, F. cumin. Cf. Kummel.

cumulate.etymology: L. cumulatus, p. p. of cumulare to heap up, fr. cumulus a heap. See Cumber.

cunctation.etymology: L. cunctatio, fr. cunctari, p.p. cunctatus, to delay.

cunctator.etymology: L., lit., a delayer; -- applied as a surname to Q. Fabius Maximus.

cuneal.etymology: L. cuneus a wege. See Coin.

cuneate.etymology: L.cuneatus, fr. cuneus a wege SeeCoin.

cuneiform.etymology: L. cuneus a wedge + -form: cf. F. cunei-forme. See Coin.

cunning.etymology: AS. cunnan to know, to be able. See 1st Con, Can.

cup.etymology: AS. cuppe, LL. cuppa cup; cf. L. cupa tub, cask; cf. also Gr. k pit, hollow, OSlav. kupa cup. Cf. Coop, Cupola, Cowl a water vessel, and Cob, Coif, Cop.

cupel.etymology: LL. cupella cup (cf. L. cupella, small cask, dim. of cupa) : cf. F. coupelle. See Cup, and cf. Coblet.

cupid.etymology: L.Cupido, fr. cupido desire, desire of love, fr. cupidus. See Cupidity.

cupidity.etymology: F. cupidite, L. cupiditas, fr. cupidus longing, desiring, fr. cupere to long for, desire. See Covet.

cupola.etymology: It. cupola, LL. cupula, cuppula (cf. L. cupula little tub). fr. cupa, cuppa, cup; cf. L. cupa tub. So called on account of its resemblance to a cup turned over. See Cup, and cf.Cupule.

cur.etymology: OE. curre, kur; cf. dial. Sw. kurre dog, OD. korre watchdog, and Icel. kurra to murmur, grumble, Sw. kurra to rumble, croak, Dan. kurre to coo, whirr; prob. of imitative origin.

curable.etymology: Cf. F. curable. See Cure, v. t.

curate.etymology: LL. curatus, prop., one who is charged with the care (L. cura) of souls. See Cure, n., and cf. Cur

curative.etymology: Cf. F.curatif. See Cure, v. t.

curator.etymology: L., fr. curare to take care of, fr. cura care.

curb.etymology: F. courber to bend, curve, L.curvare, fr. curvus bent, curved; cf. Gr. Curve.

curcuma.etymology: Cf. F., It., & Sp. curcuma; all fr. Ar. kurkum. Cf. Turmeric.

curd.etymology: Of Celtic origin; cf. Gael. gruth, Ir, gruth, cruth, curd, cruthaim I milk.

cure.etymology: OF, cure care, F., also, cure, healing, cure of souls, L. cura care, medical attendance, cure; perh. akin to cavere to pay heed, E. cution. Cure is not related to care.

curfew.etymology: OE. courfew, curfu, fr. OF. cuevrefu, covrefeu, F. couvre-feu; covrir to cover + feu fire, fr. L. focus fireplace, hearth. See Cover, and Focus.

curiosity.etymology: OE. curiouste, curiosite, OF. curioseté, curiosité, F. curiosit, fr. L. curiositas, fr. curiosus. See Currious, and cf. Curio.

curious.etymology: OF. curios, curius, F. curieux, L. curiosus careful, inquisitive, fr. cura care. See Cure.

curl.etymology: Akin to D. krullen, Dan. kr, dial. Sw. krulla to curl, crisp; possibly akin to E. crook. Cf. Curl, n., Cruller.

curlew.etymology: F. courlieu, corlieu, courlis; perh. of imitative origin, but cf. OF. corlieus courier; L. currere to run + levis light.

curmudgeon.etymology: OE. cornmudgin, where -mudgin is prob. from OF. muchier, mucier, F. musser to hide; of uncertain origin; cf. OE. muchares skulking thieves, E. miche, micher.

currant.etymology: F. corinthe (raisins de Corinthe raisins of Corinth) currant (in sense 1), from the city of Corinth in Greece, whence, probably, the small dried grape (1) was first imported, the Ribes fruit (2) receiving the name from its resemblance to that grape.

currency.etymology: Cf. LL. currentia a current, fr. L. currens, p. pr. of currere to run. See Current.

current.etymology: OE. currant, OF. curant, corant, p. pr. of curre, corre, F. courre, courir, to run, from L. currere; perh. akin to E. horse. Cf. Course, Concur, Courant, Coranto.

curry.etymology: OE. curraien, curreien, OF. cunreer, correier, to prepare, arrange, furnish, curry (a horse), F. corroyer to curry (leather) (cf. OF. conrei, conroi, order, arrangement, LL. conredium); cor- (L.com-) + roi, rei, arrangement, order; prob. of German origin, and akin to E. ready. See Ready, Greith, and cf. Corody, Array.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying with, together, etc. See Com-.

A prefix from the Latin preposition cum, signifying with, together, in conjunction, very, etc. It is used in the form com- before b, m, p, and sometimes f, and by assimilation becomes col- before l, cor- before r, and con- before any consonant except b, h, l, m, p, r, and w. Before a vowel com- becomes co-; also before h, w, and sometimes before other consonants.

curse.etymology: AS. cursian, corsian, perh. of Scand. origin; cf. Dan. korse to make the sign of the cross, Sw. korsa, fr. Dan. & Sw. kors cross, Icel kross, all these Scand. words coming fr. OF. crois, croiz, fr. L. crux cross. Cf. Cross.

cursive.etymology: LL. cursivus: cf. F. cursif See Cursitor.

cursory.etymology: L. cursorius, fr. cursor. See Cursor.

curt.etymology: L. curtus; cf. Skr. kart to cut. Cf. Curtail.

curtain.etymology: OE.cortin, curtin,fr. OF. cortine, curtine, F. courtine, LL. cortina, curtian (in senses 1 and 2), also, small court, small inclosure surrounded by walls, from cortis court. See Court.

curtal.etymology: OF. courtault, F. courtaud, having a docked tail (cf. It. cortaldo), fr. court short, L. curtus. See Curt, and Curtail.

curtilage.etymology: OF. cortillage, curtillage, fr. cortil court, courtyard, LL. cortis court. See Court.

curve.etymology: L. curvus bent, curved. See Cirb.

curvet.etymology: OE. corvet, It.corvetta: cf. F. courbette. See Curve, and cf. Corvetto.

curvilineal.etymology: L. curvus bent + E. lineal, linear.

curvilinear.etymology: L. curvus bent + E. lineal, linear.

cushion.etymology: OE. cuischun, quisshen, OF. coissin, cuissin, F. coussin, fr. (assumed) LL. culcitinum, dim. of L. culcita cushion, mattress, pillow. See Quilt, and cf. Counterpoint a coverlet.

cuspidal.etymology: From L. cuspis, cuspidis. See Cusp.

cuspidate.etymology: L. cuspidatus, p.p. of cuspidare to make pointed, fr. cuspis. See Cusp.

cuspidated.etymology: L. cuspidatus, p.p. of cuspidare to make pointed, fr. cuspis. See Cusp.

cuspidor.etymology: Pg. cuspideria, fr. cuspir to spit.

custard.etymology: Prob. the same word as OE. crustade, crustate, a pie made with a crust, fr. L. crustatus covered with a crust, p. p. of crustare, fr. crusta crust; cf. OF. croustade pasty, It. crostata, or F. coutarde. See Crust, and cf. Crustated.

custodial.etymology: Cf. F. custodial, fr. L. custodia. See Custody.

custody.etymology: L. custodia, fr. custos guard; prob. akin to Gr. hide. Seee Hide to cover.

custom.etymology: OF. custume, costume, Anglo-Norman coustome, F. coutume, fr. (assumed) LL. consuetumen custom, habit, fr. L. consuetudo, -dinis, fr. consuescere to accustom, verb inchoative fr. consuere to be accustomed; con- + suere to be accustomed, prosuus one's own; akin to E. so, adv. Cf. Consuetude, Costume.

roots.meaning: - (cum, signifying with, together, etc. See Com-.

customary.etymology: CF. OF. coustumier, F. coutumier. See Custom, and cf. Customer.

customer.etymology: A doublet of customary, a.: cf. LL. custumarius toll gatherer. See Custom.

cut.etymology: OE. cutten, kitten, ketten; prob. of Celtic origin; cf. W. cwtau to shorten, curtail, dock, cwta bobtailed, cwt tail, skirt, Gael. cutaich to shorten, curtail, dock, cutach short, docked, cut a bobtail, piece, Ir. cut a short tail, cutach bobtailed. Cf. Coot.

cutaneous.etymology: Cf. F. cutan, fr. L. cutis skin. See Cuticle.

cuticle.etymology: L. cuticula, dim. of cuttis skin; akin to E. hide skin of an animal.

cutlass.etymology: F. coutelas (cf. It. coltellaccio), augm. fr. L. cuttellus a smallknife, dim. of culter knife. See Colter, and cf. Curtal ax.

cutler.etymology: OE. coteler, F. coutelier, LL. cultellarius, fr. L. cultellus. See Cutlass.

cutlet.etymology: F. c, prop., little rib, dim. of c rib, fr. L. costa. See Coast.

cuttle.etymology: OF. cultel, coltel, coutel, fr. L. cultellus. See Cutlass.

cuttlefish.etymology: OE. codule, AS. cudele; akin to G. kuttelfish; cf. G. k, D. keutel, dirt from the guts, G. kuttel bowels, entrails. AS. cwip womb, Gith. qipus belly, womb.

cyanogen.etymology: Gr. -gen: cf. F. cyanogène. So called because it produced blue dyes.

cycas.etymology: Of uncertain origin. Linnæus derives it from one of the "obscure Greek words."

cycle.etymology: F. ycle, LL. cyclus, fr. Gr. cakra wheel, circle. See Wheel.

roots.meaning: A combining form meaning circular, of a circle or wheel.
A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

cyclopaedia.etymology: NL., from Gr. ky`klos circle + paidei`a the bringing up of a child, education, erudition, fr. paidey`ein to bring up a child. See Cycle, and cf. Encyclopedia, Pedagogue.

cyclopedia.etymology: NL., from Gr. ky`klos circle + paidei`a the bringing up of a child, education, erudition, fr. paidey`ein to bring up a child. See Cycle, and cf. Encyclopedia, Pedagogue.

cylinder.etymology: F. cylindre, OF. cilindre, L. cylindrus, fr. Gr. Calender the machine.

cymbal.etymology: OE. cimbale, simbale, OF. cimbale, F. cymbale, L. cymbalum, fr. Gr. kubha pot. Cf. Chime.

cymose.etymology: L. cymosus full of shoots: cf. FF. cymeux. See Cyme.

cymule.etymology: Cf. L. cymula a tender sprout, dim. of cyna. See Cyme.

cynic.etymology: L. cynicus of the sect of Cynics, fr. Gr. Hound.

cynical.etymology: L. cynicus of the sect of Cynics, fr. Gr. Hound.

cynosure.etymology: L. Cynosura theconstellation Cynosure, Gr. Cynic.

cypress.etymology: OE. cipres, cipresse, OF. cipres, F. cypr, L. cupressus, cyparissus (cf. the usual Lat. form cupressus), fr. Gr. g, Gen. vi. 14.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

cypripedium.etymology: NL., fr. Cypris Venus + pes, pedis, foot.

cyprus.etymology: OE. cipres, cypirs; perh. so named as being first manufactured in Cyprus. Cf. Cipers.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.
Combining forms fr. Gr. li`qos a stone; -- used chiefly in naming minerals and rocks.

czar.etymology: Russ. tsare, fr. L. Caesar Cæsar; cf. OPol. czar, Pol. car.

czarina.etymology: Cf. G. Zarin, Czarin, fem., Russ. tsaitsa.
